utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed that there were technical problems, but now that they have been resolved we can start. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I have mentioned it to the Chamber's legal officer. I apologise for not having the documents on Friday, when I argued the admissibility of cross-examination of Mr. Zaric on the -- what was contained in those Omri, that's the o-m-r-i transcripts. Since then I have -- or it has been brought to my attention there is a filing in this case which is relevant to Your Honour's determination which is a filing on the 28th of May, 1997 entitled, "Report on measures taken by the Prosecutor for the personal service of the indictment and warrants of arrest." It's a 61A -- Rule 61A report back to the Chamber of May 1997. It's at pages D403 to -- sorry, D400 to D403. There were three relevant portions there, referring to publication of the interview and the conversation with Mr. Pantelic who was then acting for the accused as to service of the indictments. I have copies here for Your Honours if you don't have them in court with the filings. I have also found the Omri interview which was actually published on the 19th of November, 1996, in the Balkan -- in an analytical brief, volume 1, number -- number 1, number -- sorry, volume 1, number 46 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is the same interview which the accused had indicated that it should be shown to his counsel before publication?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's part of the interview. It's a media interview. It's not -- it's obviously not the transcript. That's not a media interview. It is an interview on finding Mr. Zaric and some things he had said in relation to the indictment and in relation to organised -- who organised the mass isolation or ethnic cleansing of Bosanski Samac. So it had -- parts of it had been published. Parts of Mr. Zaric's comments on the interview and the allegations put to him have been published and were published in 1996. So I think that's in answer to Her Honour Judge Williams's specific question as to whether or not there was publication and the extent of it. I have the article here if Your Honours wish to see it for the purpose of your determination and how far the Prosecution should be permitted, if at all, to go in cross-examining Mr. Zaric, as to things he has said which are in the media. So if it's convenient, I can hand up copies of the publication and spare copies of the filing of 28th of May, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you wait, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll hand up three copies of the filing of 28th of May and three copies of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. If I just have a brief opportunity to address the Chamber with regard to certain part of submission of my learned friend Mr. Re. If you see, Your Honours, in the document which was just provided to you, it's a report of our learned colleague Ms. Nancy Paterson. At that time she was legal advisor for the Office of the Prosecution. On page 400 - actually, this is page 4 of her report that you have in front of you - speaking of alleged meeting on 20 of February 1997, it is very clear said in the report -- I will make a quotation. "Nancy Paterson, legal officer of the OTP, had a meeting with Borislav Pisarevic, co-defence counsel with Igor Pantelic for Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric, in Bosanski Samac. At said meeting, Mr. Pisarevic confirmed again that Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric have received copies of the indictment," and so on and so forth. Well, learning -- reading this particular portion, no one can understand that there was a meeting between Ms. Paterson, myself, and my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic. It's rather a description that my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic acted at that time as a co-defence counsel with me, in terms of his capacity. That's number one. Although all these issues are not so relevant. My learned friend Mr. Pisarevic will add something in support of our clarification of this situation. So just for the record, Your Honour, I want to be -- that everything would be clear. And in conclusion, I never was with Ms. Paterson at that meeting on that date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. With regard to this, I'd merely like to say the following: I am not aware that Nancy Paterson was in Bosanski Samac in 1997, that she visited me there, and that we discussed this subject. We possibly talked over the telephone. And although we were aware of the indictments, but we never received them. Perhaps we did, but from what I can recollect, it was from the press that we photocopied the indictment, part of that indictment. So that in 1997, the indictment was not served on Mr. Zaric or given to me or any one of us. I'm certain about that. And as for the relevance, this interview that the Prosecutor is talking about was done in November 1996. So even if we had some information in 1997, because in 1995 we learnt that there was an indictment. But I do not think that can affect the decision of the court. So that now I really cannot say that I told Mrs. Nancy Paterson that we had received the indictment. Yes, we knew it, but we never received it in total. It was given us the first time by Mr. Miroslav Tadic and Mr. Milan Simic were arrested at the SFOR base in Dubrave next to Tuzla. It was then that OTP representatives delivered the indictment to us for the first time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will make its ruling after the break. It would like to look at the submissions further. You can continue with other areas of your cross-examination, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Pisarevic, we -- the Trial Chamber has been informed that it hasn't been possible to have the Rule 92 statement of Mr. Nizam Ramusovic certified yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe that the Trial Chamber is fully informed about all the measures that have been undertaken in relation to the certification of Mr. Nizam Ramusovic's statement, according to Rule 92 bis. We were informed by the registry that it is -- that the best possible way to do it is through the administration of the United States, and I had close contacts with Mr. Weiner, being American citizen and a lawyer from the United States, I furthermore sent a couple of letters to the American Embassy, to their legal counsellor, asking for some advice for help in organising that. What we find -- we find his statement very important for our case, particularly having in mind the positions that the Prosecution has expressed in their response to our filings in our motions for judicial acquittal. So we believe that there is still a possibility that someone from the registry, just the way it happened on two occasions when they went to Samac and did the certification of statements, someone from the registry, the assigned officer of the registry could go to California and certify his statement. Latest development regarding Mr. Ramusovic himself is that Mr. Pisarevic spoke to him on Saturday and he is waiting for someone to approach him for certifying this 92 bis statement. So whatever should be decided by the registry, whether we could proceed with what we are doing now and trying to get certification through the authorities of the United States or the assigned officer from the registry should go there, whatever they find appropriate, we are fine with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The position is that it has not been possible to have the statement certified through the assistance of the Prosecution, through their state department. So the Trial Chamber is asking the registry to send a Presiding Officer to have the statement certified as we approach the closing of the case. We'll proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zaric please be provided with copies of his records of interview or statements to the OTP, Exhibits P141 and 142 ter. And maybe if they could be left with him, because I will be referring to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric. Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Last week and the week before, you gave evidence of your second trip to Belgrade. Now, you said that was in, I think, late May, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to take you to, if you could possibly look at P140 ter, which is the interview of the 1st of April, 1998, at page 76 and 77.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have P140 in front of me. I have P141 and 142, but not P140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the accused please be given P140.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. To be clear, I was required to provide the accused with 141 and 142. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I have it before me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could just turn, please, to pages 76 and 77.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just read to yourself from about halfway down the page, from where it says "Nancy," that's Ms. Paterson, saying: "So Mr. Tadic came in his role as a member of the Crisis Staff." Just read to yourself down to the bottom of the page. I'll just ask to make sure that you've found the passage I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have page 77 before me. Is that the page you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Please start on page 76, about a third of the way down. There's a break and it says: "Nancy: So Mr. Tadic --"

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could just read that to yourself down to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You see at the bottom the last question, where

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON SAYS
utterances.text: "Why did you go to Belgrade and not Radovan Antic? He was head of the 4th Detachment." To which your answer is, over the page,

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC
utterances.text: "I was in charge of security and I was chief of this department for national security. Therefore, I was appointed there by the Crisis Staff, so I had to. I did not stay very long in this position and they replaced me fairly rapidly." Next question, Ms. Paterson: "All this happened somewhere around the end of May; correct?" Answer, your answer: "Yes." All I simply ask you is: You adhere to the answer that you gave to the Prosecutor there, that the reason you went with the Crisis Staff was because you were in charge of security and chief of this department of national security, and that's why you went to Belgrade with them at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was only my comment, which was not finished in this interview. I am deeply convinced that the real reason was a scenario that had been prepared, not the fact that I was the chief for national security, and that I was working in the area of security. I was just beginning to comment on this for Mrs. Nancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you're saying that that's an incomplete answer, but at the time you went there, you were the chief of the department of national security and that was part of the scenario which the Crisis Staff was preparing, or part of the scenario that had been prepared?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that, as I have already testified here - and I will repeat again - I had objections to my appointment, or rather, I was commenting on my appointment as chief of national security. This was purely a formal fact, because I never actually did anything in that capacity, nor did I ever do any work or submit any reports either to the Crisis Staff or to anybody else which might put me in a direct relationship with the Crisis Staff. My reaction was that I had been appointed, but the technological issues concerning the service had not been resolved, and I went to Pale for consultations about this. At the first session of the Crisis Staff, this item was taken off the agenda in a manner in which I testified to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking at the transcript, and I believe that we have something here that doesn't make much sense. Maybe Mr. Re can clarify this right now. On page 6, on question, on line 13, Mr. Re asked Mr. Zaric: "Last week and the week before, you gave evidence of your second trip to Belgrade. Now, you said that was in, I think, late May, didn't you?" And the answer of Mr. Zaric was: "Yes, on the 9th of May." So I just wanted to make sure that they are talking about one and the same trip to Belgrade, because we know that there were two trips, and Mr. Zaric here referred to his first trip on 9th of May, and I believe that Mr. Re is asking about the second trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you heard what Mr. Lazarevic just said. Clearly, I was referring to the second trip, which was the one in late May, when you went there with Mr. Simic and Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Tadic and met Mr. Bogdanovic there, not the first trip in relation to Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then it's not the 9th of May; it's the meeting that was held in late May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I actually asked you and that's what I directed your attention to. And the question was: Why did you go to Belgrade and not Radovan Antic? He was the head of the 4th Detachment. To which you answered: I was in charge of security and I was chief of this department of national security, et cetera. And then the next question which I read to you was: "All this happened somewhere around the end of May; correct?" And you answered, yes. Are you completely clear about what you're talking about there is the second trip to Belgrade, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is: You adhere to the answer you gave to the Prosecutor in the presence of your lawyer that the reason, even if it's an incomplete answer, the reason that you went to Belgrade in late May instead of Radovan Antic was that you were in charge of security and you were chief of the department of national security and you were appointed by the Crisis Staff and you had to go, as part of a scenario or for whatever reason, and that was in late May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to repeat to Their Honours that I simply tried to give Mrs. Nancy Paterson a comment, which we did not enlarge upon in our further interview. And my assumption as to why they put me in that scenario was the fact that I was performing the duty of assistant commander for security and they formally appointed me chief for national security, where I had certain reserves from the beginning -- certain reservations from the very beginning, but the fact that I went to Belgrade had to show Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Tadic that I could see what sort of contacts Mr. Todorovic had with some people in Belgrade, in very high places, and in the period that followed, there was intense pressure on me to continue keeping silent and not to resist or offer any resistance to what was being done. On that occasion, Mrs. Nancy seemed not to be interested in going further into this issue, which is why we did not say what I have just told the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no. Look, the question I'm directing your mind to is the question and answer you gave, and I understand you wish to elaborate on it, and that's fine, and you didn't give as full a version as you possibly could have to Ms. Paterson. But what you said when she asked you a very short, direct question, why did you go to Belgrade and not Radovan Antic, you said: I was in charge of security and I was chief of this department of national security. Therefore, I was appointed there by the Crisis Staff, so I had to. You then said you didn't stay very long in the position, and it was at the end of May. All I'm asking you is: You adhere, don't you, to what you said to the Prosecutor, and you told her the truth then, that the end of May you were in charge of security and was chief of this department for national security, whether nominally or not. I'm just saying you adhere to the truthful answer that you gave to the Prosecutor, don't you, as to your title when you went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Re, what I have just said in my previous answer, that's my definite response. I have no other reply to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you meant something different to: I was chief of this department for national security, when you told the Prosecutor, on the 1st of April, 1998, that, as of the end of May you were "chief of this department for national security"? Are you saying those plain, simple words mean something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those words meant nothing else but the fact that my, conditionally speaking, posts that I held at the time were the basis for my being taken there with them for me to see the entire scenario in Belgrade, and then for me to be put under pressure at the local level. It was in this context that I mentioned these words. But your esteemed colleague Nancy Paterson was not interested in the rest of this story, and that's why I'm putting it forward now, because I'm being given the chance to explain why I thought there was this scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're not being given the chance to explain. I was asking you simply about your title at the time. So it will be much quicker for all of us if you can just concentrate on that part of the question, and you answered it before you started talking further. So please confine yourself. You could have given me that answer ten minutes ago. Now, Mr. Zaric, I want to move on to another area. Can you just turn the interview over, please. Mr. Zaric, last week I asked you some questions about Mr. Tihic, and the radio interview with Mr. Tihic. As well as Mr. Tihic, of course, you said was a person you had known for a long time and you described the radio interview as part of the humiliation which was being perpetrated against him. Remember that evidence? I think it was on Friday.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I used the word "humiliation," but I do remember I said that it was part of the pressure being put on Mr. Tihic. If I did use that word, I would like you to quote that part to me. But in any case, I think that there was an improper scenario put in place for Mr. Tihic to speak on the radio. As far as I heard, this was on the 19th, but I also heard that he had already spoken on the 18th, so that this statement of his was broadcast on several occasions by means of a tape and certain technology used in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic's humiliation at the hands of the Serb -- the new Serb authorities continued with the television interview, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was continued with pressure put on him. Whether this amounts to humiliation, I wouldn't say that in this context. But in any case, there was special psychological pressure put on him, because he had arrived from detention to give an interview, and therefore I agree with you that these were unfavourable circumstances for Mr. Tihic as the leader of a party at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, this special psychological pressure on him continued throughout the time he was in custody, didn't it, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You're correct there. I share your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you wrote about Mr. Tihic's television interview in your book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote about that interview in my book. I was very critical and I believe that I was very correct in the way I described it, if that means anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to paraphrase, you described it as a staged inscripted interview, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tihic [sic] be given that copy of the book again, if my learned friends have it? I'm sorry, Mr. Zaric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think you'll find it on about page 251?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have found page 251. If that's the part where there are photographs in the -- on the top of the page and some text on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. Just give me one moment. I'll find my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. It's Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm getting there. I'm getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's in the chapter entitled "slapdash state." And according to the English version, it's around -- it's underneath the heading "2," which is around page 251, with the photographs of Mr. Tihic, Mr. Nalic, Mr. Hadzialijagic, and Mr. Nikolic, possibly the page before. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is. Just tell me what you want and then I'll find my way around. When you tell me what you want me to comment on or to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to have a look, from where it says, "The reportage was organised by the Crisis Staff." That's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to read a passage to you, and it goes like this: "The reportage was organised by the Crisis Staff. Together with the reporter and the cameraman, they decided what should be the most important message of the events in Samac. A general frame was agreed on. During the filming itself, military and political cliches increasingly stifled the basic need to present the events themselves and the intentions of the Muslims and Croats in a simple --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Re, please. Or could we have the book on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought I provided the interpreters with a copy of this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe they haven't -- when did you provide? This morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Friday. It was page 101 of the English. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't think we can find that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe what you can do is slow down, read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "And the intentions of the Muslims and Croats in a simple, clear, effective and convincing manner. When nationalist rhetoric was thrown on top of everything as a crowning glory, the result was`great,' but only to our own mind. And we had no sense of what looks good on television, nor experience enough to approach the events from the viewers' angle. In this kind of script it was decided beforehand who would say what and what had to be shown. This helped kill spontaneity even further. Everything was mixed up. The authors of the programme yielded to the demands and cliches of the Crisis Staff, while the Crisis Staff presumptuously got involved in writing and directing, which was why the result was problematic. During the shooting, it turned out that the central place in the programme was somehow given to intelligence, although that had not been the intention. Intelligence agents do not get their pictures taken, nor do they talk much, if at all. But my superior commands's orders put me in a situation where I had to tell a story which would unmask the Croat-Muslim coalition, its conspiracy against the Serbs, its armament and preparations for war. Material that incriminated the coalition and that had only been discovered a day earlier was thrust into my hands in no particular order, and I barely had time to give it a cursory glance (even though I had to talk about it and refer to it) so that I could neither -- so sorry, I could be neither systematic or entirely logical. "My position was made especially unpleasant and emotionally tough by the decision of the `writers and directors' to bring the detainees, Tihic, Izetbegovic, Nalic, and Hadzialijagic, to the programme. Sunglasses had to be found for Izetbegovic and Nalic in order to conceal their bruises as much as possible. According to the script, they too would be part of `my segment,' where we would, so to speak, confront each other at a kind of round table, and they were asked to confess before the cameras what they had planned and done against the Serbs. Unfortunately, I was on more or less good terms with these men, and Tihic was my friend. Our writers thought this was perfect, the best way to illustrate the depths to which Bosnia and Herzegovina had sunk. Friend facing friend, as investigator and criminal! That is why I was confused and ill at ease, flustered in front of the camera. My throat was dry and my words and thoughts popped up in no logical sequence." I read that correctly to you, didn't I, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, you read for a long time, and there are many words and many things not properly translated from the B/C/S, as it stands here. I don't know where you found those words, which are not here in the book. I would now have to spend about ten minutes reading out page 250 in order to convince the Chamber that the things said here were not what you read out. I heard quite a few things which are not mentioned here at all, and yet you uttered them. Whether it's a matter of translation or something else, I can't go into that, but the essence was not brought into question. There are, however, many words and sentences which are not in here, and you said them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I was reading from the official English translation provided by the ICTY's interpreters of that passage in your book. I don't want you to go into it too much, but is there anything I read out which changes the meaning or the gist of what you read? And perhaps you could just highlight whatever I read out that has somehow changed the meaning of what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't change the meaning. It's a critical description of all this and the essence is the same, but there are many sentences and words not mentioned in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm asking you: Are any of those -- bearing in mind that it's an interpretation of my reading it out and not a translation, are there any words I used which have changed the meaning or are important to you to get across what the book actually says, that are different, any words that I read out that are different to what you were reading in the book that makes an important change to your meaning?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, as you read it, you mentioned Mr. Tihic's name, but in the beginning there is absolutely no mention of that man. And there were also some other words which were put there. Now I'm not all that focused to be able to associate the words that you uttered and those which do not exist in this version. But now, if I were to read this version, and this is the original, written in B/C/S, and then if I did that, you would see that many things deviate from what you've just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't actually mention Mr. Tihic at the beginning, and I don't know how that could have crept in. But what I'm asking you is: Was there anything which to you was important?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it is important that what I've said be interpreted and be translated as I put it. The English version has turned things in a different direction slightly. But I want to say that the critical substance of my wish, which I wanted to present in this book, has not been brought into question fully. That is, it has not gone beyond my principled framework, and therefore I do not mind if we go on talking about this subject if I keep this critical approach, as I have just indicated to you to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've seen the first paragraph, where it says, about -- in the 1, 2, 3 -- I think fourth sentence: "When nationalist rhetoric was thrown on top of everything." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just so there's no difference in what we're saying to each other, can you just read out that one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, as icing on the cake, the national rhetoric was spread over all it, it turned out "quite well." This word "quite well" is in inverted commas and it is not by accident that I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but only following our line of thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Well, I just want to ask you about that line. The English interpretation -- I'm sorry, translation as opposed to interpretation in inverted commas is great as opposed to quite well. But I'm not going to make anything of that. But what I want to ask you is simply this: What do you mean by "when nationalist rhetoric was --" my translation says, "thrown on top of everything," but you said, "icing on the cake or as a crowning glory, the result was quite -- looked quite well or was great." What did you mean by the result looked quite well or great to our own eyes or our own mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When some questions were put to people who participated in that TV programme, and by this I primarily mean Mr. Tihic, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Nalic, and Mr. Hadzialijagic, to my mind, one could not but conclude that some questions did not go in that direction; that is, they did not bring into the forefront the Serb position of sorts. And then to -- followed by what would -- could be associated with those people who were not Serbs. It was within that context that I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The questions and answers, as part of this nationalist rhetoric put to -- I withdraw the question in that form. The questions put to Mr. Tihic and the others as part of that nationalist rhetoric, and the answers he gave, or they gave, were part of the humiliation that these men were subjected to by this television interview, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that what they said in their interview was not a lie. They uttered very many truths. But the question that arises in my mind is under what circumstances and under what conditions did they tell that story. Because if Mr. Tihic or any other of the participants said and confirmed that before the war they had been arming themselves illegally, had their paramilitary formations, and so on and so forth, then that is something that I and others were aware of. The question only arises whether, at the moment when people were put in front of the camera, was a correct one, because they were telling the truth and yet had come out of detention. And it is in that context that I think some kind of a democratic relationship, because it was -- it was in the media, has not been issued [phoen], because they did not say why they had armed, were they afraid of somebody or whatever. So that other side and an opportunity for them to say something else in front of the cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. Please. Please concentrate. I'm going to ask it this way: These people as you knew had been detained, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they had been mistreated in detention, hadn't they? They had been beaten, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before they came to participate in the television programme?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it happened at the time before that. But they were not -- and I testified about it. But they were not beaten that day or those who came from Brcko. I know that there was no ill-treatment there. But during the previous period, from their detention onward, yes, they had been subjected to ill-treatment. That is an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You of course refer to this in your book, where you say that -- well, in effect: They had been beaten so much that "sunglasses had to be found for Izetbegovic and Nalic in order to conceal their bruises as much as possible."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But these bruises dated back to some earlier beating, not beating that day. And I think that you don't think of that same day either, that you also think that they had been exposed to some torture before that. And the fact that these two gentlemen had glasses on their heads, as said, so that these bruises would be less obvious, less visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why, by your last answer, are you trying to minimise the beatings or the effect of the beatings on these men, by saying it didn't occur on the day? Why are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understood you to be saying that before they were brought to the cameras, that they had been beaten. And I'm saying that that is not in dispute, but that it had not happened on that day that they had been exposed to mistreatment -- the previous days. And far be it from me to refute the fact that they had been beaten earlier. Perhaps you misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I don't. But how does it matter, for the purposes of their humiliation by their Serb captors, in front of the TV with this scripted interview whether they had in fact been beaten that day or beaten on an earlier day, yet had to have sunglasses put on them to conceal their bruises? How does that matter, Mr. Zaric, in the context of what happened to them? It doesn't, does it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no, it doesn't, but that is how I understood your question, and I merely tried to answer it somewhat more precisely. But if you want me to speculate, then I agree with you: There is absolutely no reason why I should bring into doubt that they had been under specific circumstances and that they had been mistreated before that. I am not trying to refute that or to challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They were being used by the Serb authorities who had taken over the town as a propaganda tool, weren't they, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serb authorities, is a rather broad term, because I know that that TV crew had arrived from Novi Sad. But now when I think of the programme as a whole very correctly, I believe that it more or less did contain that message which you mentioned in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you agreeing with what I just said to you, what I just asked you? The question: They were being used by the Serb authorities, who had taken over the town as a propaganda tool? Are you agreeing with that question I just put to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have my opinion about that programme, and I'm not bringing it into question. What was carried by Novi Sad television was carried for the whole of Yugoslavia and the whole of Yugoslavia and the whole world, so that programme, whether the Serb authorities in Samac of all places, with all that powerful to direct it as they wanted so as to fit it into their official policy or whether they wanted to see it in a broader context, that is something I do not know and cannot give you a precise opinion about that [as interpreted]. But whatever the case, to my mind, this programme had a negative approach because I think it is not correct and it is not all right for people to give interviews under such specific conditions which are called prison camp, battery, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You agreed earlier that the interview was staged and scripted, and in your book, you said the reportage was organised by the Crisis Staff. Your evidence has been, and in your statements, that the Crisis Staff took over Bosanski Samac. Putting those things together, the Crisis Staff organising this, bringing the detainees from custody, scripting the interview, having prominent Muslims used in the context of nationalist rhetoric, those Serb authorities were using them as a propaganda tool, weren't they, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the word and said it was directed or orchestrated by the Crisis Staff, on the basis of information that I had and that I did not question, that namely Stevan Todorovic, as a member of the Crisis Staff, and that is what I think of him, through some connections of his, had orchestrated their participation. And as for the interview itself, you can see it here, because that tape is an exhibit. The journalist who conducted the interview asked the questions himself. I do not believe that he wasn't a man polished enough so as to be unable to ask questions himself. But the whole programme, to my mind, acquired a rather negative tone, a negative intonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: According to your book, you said that the Crisis Staff were the "writers and directors." And it was their decision to bring the detainees to the interview. That is, the Crisis Staff staged and scripted this interview for their own purposes. Those purposes were to use these men as a propaganda tool, weren't they? Could you please just focus on that question. I've asked it several times and you've gone round and round and round but haven't focused on it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only too well who were the masterminds in the Crisis Staff. I know that well. But I am not disputing the fact that you want me to tell, namely, that Boro Simeunovic [as interpreted] and Ninkovic who to my mind were the ideologues so were the masterminds together with Stevan Todorovic that they wrote the script and they gave it to me and to journalists who came to make that programme. That programme also includes interviews with townsmen from Samac who also gave some positive assessments as to what was going on in the territory of the town at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct here in transcript on page 23, line 22, here it says that Simeunovic and there was one name missing here. That's Ninkovic, what Mr. Zaric said. But he didn't say Simeunovic. The only Simeunovic we have here is Mr. Makso Simeunovic, and he has nothing to do with this interview. So he said Simeun Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may, on the same topic: I don't believe that we heard that Mr. Zaric said that -- but I -- this is line 21: "But I'm not disputing the fact that you want me to tell," et cetera, et cetera. It's rather ambiguous and imprecise. It was not correctly interpreted what Mr. Zaric said. Reading this part of his statement, for Mr. Zaric, it is not in dispute that someone from Crisis Staff made all this scenario, questions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. I think I'll just ask through Mr. Re that the answer be repeated slowly, so that we have all the names correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I might ask it more simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, this is a very, very simple question. Who wrote the script you just referred to, just the names, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who wrote the script, but I'm telling you that I know who were the brain fathers behind all this writing and certain things in the Crisis Staff, and I mentioned the names of Mr. Simeun Simic and Bozo Ninkovic. But I did not see the two of them making that script. Had I seen them, I would have told you, because there is no reason for me to hide it. All I can do is speculate and make assumptions and say: Well, they sat down and talked it out, and so on and so forth. But whether that is correct and whether such a statement will be relevant as a truth here before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Good morning, Mr. Zaric. There is a slight discrepancy between your two answers. In the first one you mentioned also Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and in the latter answer you mentioned only two persons, Mr. Simic and Mr. Ninkovic. What about Mr. Todorovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think that Mr. Todorovic is a brain father, if you understand what I mean. But nonetheless, he should be included in that script. And I did not mean to keep him out of that script. But he's not one of those people, as far as I know him. I've never seen him sit down and write half a page of anything. He's simply not that kind of man. I'm not trying to underestimate him, whether he knows how to do it or not, but since I know those other two, I can say that they were the ones who, in a certain way, and on behalf of the Crisis Staff, they wrote, published certain things and had them carried by radio and other media, which the Crisis Staff at the time used as its organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in all of the circumstances which you have described in your book as to the participation of the men having been brought from detention, wearing sunglasses, a script written by the Crisis Staff for Muslims to answer questions asked by Serbs, the participation of these men in that interview could not be described as voluntary, could it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you knew that at the time when they were there being interviewed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Despite that, you chose to participate in the process, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Re, in any war, there is a situation where a foot soldier or an NCO does not choose what he will do. He simply carries out orders. And I was very unhappy about it, and I'm telling you honestly about this, but the question is whether Simo Zaric had been trusted. It was very reluctantly that I took part in that programme, and I endeavoured as much as I could to help create a more normal atmosphere, an atmosphere of normalcy so that these people could say what they thought in a normal atmosphere. And Mr. Tihic through Mr. Sarkanovic asked me to stay there throughout so that nothing would happen to them. So that was the reason why I was there, and I carried out the order of my superior commander and I made a contribution to this television programme which is amongst the exhibits here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This interview was one of the many acts of humiliation and discrimination committed against the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac by those authorities in charge in April 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep talking about the factor of humiliation. That is not in question. But I would rather be ready to accept the fact that it was an incorrect psychological pressure to which these people were exposed, who, bearing in mind the circumstances they had come from detention and gave their interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This use of these men as a propaganda tool was designed to further the Serb cause in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it, and in fact throughout Yugoslavia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this kind of propaganda that you mention is something that I gave least thought at the time when I was tasked to give my opinion about the material that I referred to in the interview. And that there were such television and other programmes, that there were hundreds of them in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is a well-known fact. But it does not mean, however, that this interview did not take place in a very poor psychological atmosphere. Of course, when it comes to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, when it comes to non-Serbs, you participated in the interview knowing that these detained Muslim captives were being used as a propaganda tool by the Serb authorities in Bosanski Samac. There's no other explanation for what was happening, was there -- is there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I put that conclusion down in my book in 1999. At that moment, I wasn't thinking about that type of the script, who and what was pursued by the person who brought that team. In that programme, all I did was what I had been ordered by my superior, and I could see beyond any doubt that those others participating in that programme were in much more disadvantaged position than, for instance, I, who gave my part of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your participation in that interview process assisted the Serb authorities in their campaign of humiliation and propaganda against the Muslims and non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean by this that I accepted such a script from the outset, or is it the fact which I wish to present to the Trial Chamber that I had been given the task by my superior to participate in that programme? Now I'm clear too, Mr. Re, that that programme - and I wish it had never been aired and that I had not participated in it, although I had no choice, because I could not choose which order to obey and which not to obey. I think that this was a propaganda, that its character was adverse, and I stand by that. But I did not participate deliberately, that is, I did not want to contribute to the humiliation, discrimination [phoen] or degradation of anything that has to do with non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you accept the mere fact of your participation in that process did advance the Serb campaign of humiliation and discrimination against non-Serbs, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broadcast was seen on television twice, and then it was never aired again. Whether it made such a deep impression on people's memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, please. The question was: You accept, don't you, that the mere fact of your participation in that process did advance the Serb campaign of humiliation and discrimination against non-Serbs, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a single moment do I want to deny that a critical attitude should be taken to that television broadcast. What conclusion will be drawn in the end from my participation, I will not go into now. I do not deny that the broadcast had negative connotations. My intention was certainly not what you are talking about. There is no denying that I took part, that I was drawn into it, but it did have negative effect and I do not deny that. I was even more severe in my criticism of it in my book than you are being now in your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we take our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has a ruling on this issue of the interviews and the plan by the Prosecution to use them. The Trial Chamber has considered the submissions of the parties on the use of the interviews of the 12th and 16th November 1996 by the accused Simo Zaric with Jan Urban and Yvonne Badal of the Omri in Sarajevo. The Trial Chamber has decided not to allow the Prosecution to refer to the said interviews, as the circumstances of the interviews, notwithstanding their publication as such, that their probative value is substantially outweighed by the need it ensure a fair trial. So the Prosecution cannot refer to them. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've still got your book in front of you. Please just turn to page 323. It's the second paragraph after the divider 2. Do you see the first paragraph says: "When I had the indictment in my hands." The next one says: "As for Blagoje Simic ..."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Last Thursday, Mr. Pantelic cross-examined you and asked you about the participation of Mr. -- or Dr. Simic and what you had seen of him in Bosanski Samac during the war. The second paragraph of your book here, at page 235 of the English and 323 of the original says: "As for Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic, their functions and characters say something about them. The former, Simic, was a hard-line politician, fiercely nationalistic, the latter, that's Todorovic, a rigid man, appointed chief of police in evil times and with insufficient training." That's what you said in your book. I've quoted that correctly, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says something similar. Not exactly the same, but about the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of things led you to conclude that Dr. Simic was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic? Was it the policies of the Crisis Staff and their involvement in ethnic cleansing or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't connect this right away to ethnic cleansing. I think that Mr. Blagoje Simic never concealed the fact that he was a Serb nationalist. He didn't talk much. I was not in a situation to participate in many meetings that he attended, but if I were to refer to the assembly held on the 26th or the 16th - I can't remember exactly - of December, 1992, when there was a certain debate concerning the information we have mentioned, and as he was actually chairing that session, I saw him as a person who responded very harshly, in my view, to anything that was not totally in line with the official SDA policy, or the policy of the authorities in the municipality. From this I drew a conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- SDA, you meant SDS, didn't you? It's translated as SDA. You said SDS, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter made a mistake. The witness said SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please continue. From this, I drew a conclusion -- just continue the answer: From this, I drew a conclusion ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew the conclusion that I knew Mr. Blagoje Simic only slightly before the war. When the authorities in Samac were set up and when the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board, who were the representatives of the authorities in the narrowest sense of the word, showed what they were like in practice, I think that Mr. Blagoje Simic was surrounded by people who were seen more as Serbian nationalists than he was in public. I think that he took on his duty at a very difficult point in time, and it may not be proper for me to say this, but I think he was simply not up to the job. And around him were people who were already seasoned politicians, who, in my view, constantly held him in a checkmate position, and that is why I have the impression that the responses of the Crisis Staff to certain challenges could not have been done better when I look at who was there with him and who the people were whom Blagoje, as the president of the Crisis Staff, trusted. The line of fierce national and in some individuals nationalistic policy was something I experienced in the way I have described, thinking that he perhaps should have had the strength to resist if he was under pressure from the demands of individuals surrounding him. In my view, there was no doubt that some individuals, like Milan Simic, Simeun Simic, Bozo Ninkovic, Stevan Todorovic, and so on, did not hesitate to show what their policy was, and I disagreed with it, in spite of the fact that it was wartime --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've been going about five minutes on something which you wrote very simply and if I might say so eloquently in your book. As for Blagoje Simic, the former was a hard-line politician, fiercely nationalistic. What I want ask you is: You've expressed an opinion based upon a conclusion. Was it Dr. Simic's participation in a shadow or parallel Serb government which took over the town and imposed discriminatory, persecutory policies on the population and on Serb population? Was that one of the things that lead you to conclude that he was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, because term used by my learned friend from Prosecution office, "shadow government," "parallel," et cetera, is absolutely inappropriate. I know that this is Prosecution theory and Prosecution case, but Mr. Zaric is not a constitutional law expert. He is not a legal expert, Your Honour. And we shall provide enough evidences in our closing arguments that we cannot speak about the shadow or parallel government, given the fact that the Bosnia-Herzegovina was in a process of dissolution, starting at the mid-of October 1991, where the constitutional principles were violated. So that's a matter for submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You've put it very well that you make those points in your concluding arguments, and you had better do that. And please sit down. There is nothing wrong with the question posed by the Prosecution. These are matters that have been discussed with most of the witnesses, and even with Mr. Simo Zaric himself. So he can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in your own evidence, you've described the Serbian Samac municipality as a parallel government, sometime last week. What I'm asking you is: Was it Dr. Simic's participation in this shadow or parallel Serb government which took over the town and imposed discriminatory, persecutory policies on the non-Serb population, was that one of the things that led you to conclude that Dr. Simic was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a distinction in my reply. The first part of your question, relating to, as you say, a shadow government, although I'm no legal expert, I have my political viewpoint on this, as an individual. I was never in favour of ethnic grouping, and this is my standpoint which I will never change.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you answer the question now, please. I'm talking about Dr. Simic and his participation. Was that one of the things that caused you to conclude that he was fiercely hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic? So to save time, please just answer that question, and not some other one that you want to answer, and please just concentrate on that one.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just coming to this, to your question, that is. The establishment of the Serbian municipality of Samac, according to the information that became available in February, and the second session of the assembly that was held in late March, was indubitably part of the policy supported [Realtime transcript omitted the word "supported"] by Dr. Blagoje Simic. This is deep conviction and that is something I disagreed with and will never agree with. If Dr. Blagoje Simic's participation in this kind of policy of organising a Serbian municipality along ethnic lines is to be treated as a hard-line policy, then I agree with this. I don't want to enter into constitutional or other issues than topical on the territory of Republika Srpska. The consequences of this policy, which later emerged, are something quite different. I cannot claim here that I ever heard, in my whole life, Blagoje Simic ordering any act of discrimination to be carried out. In practice, however, I know that there were things that were improper and inhumane in relation to the non-Serb population, and I feel that there was discrimination, especially in the case of some individuals. Which individuals contributed to bringing these people into this situation where they were discriminated against, I think this can be personified quite clearly as said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Page 34, line 1, we heard that after the word policy Mr. Zaric said supported, and then it continuing by -- with word by Blagoje Simic, et cetera. Just for the sake of precision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You've seen the point, Mr. Re, the line? That's line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The word "supported" is missing from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you accept Mr. Pantelic's correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you see, you've concluded that he was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic. And you've said a moment ago that the consequences of this policy later emerged. The truth is that the consequences of this policy of establishing a parallel government and taking over the municipality in fact emerged on the 17th of April, 1992, the date on which Muslims and Croats were rounded up -- the beginning -- the start -- the commencement day of the rounding up and arrest and detention of Muslims and Croats in Bosanski Samac and your own evidence has been of what you did by taking them to Brcko on the 26th of April. So you'd accept that these consequences emerged very, very shortly after the takeover, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also said a moment ago that it was Dr. Simic's participation in a meeting, I think you said in December 1992, where he had a particularly hard-line to those who opposed SDS policies. You're aware, of course, of the SDS policy proclaimed in the six strategic objectives, which is P5 in evidence here, one of which is establishing state borders, separating the Serb people from the other two ethnic communities. Was it his support for that particular SDS policy that led you to conclude that he was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic? And please answer it as simply as you can.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be sincere and say that the document on the strategic goals adopted by the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska is something I saw for the first time when it was disclosed here. Therefore, I could not talk about the overall policy. I can talk about what happened in practice on the ground, when the Serbian municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation was established. It then became evident that the Serbian national factor dominated in politics, and generally. There was no action by non-Serbs. Therefore, I feel that if new forces coming into power in a multiparty system pretending to be democrats, then they should have given the opportunity to others to take part in political life. This would have been normal, that all people who live there could participate. That's how I see things, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. A moment ago you agreed that -- or you had accepted that the consequences you referred to earlier emerged very shortly after the takeover, and I've referred to the rounding up of Muslims and Croats, their arrest, and all the other things that happened, the isolation and so on. Now, of course, you were aware of that, but by the very fact of your intervention by taking prisoners to Brcko on the 26th of April, you were aware of the emergence of those consequences of discriminatory behaviour as of the 26th of April, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of April? You mean when those people went to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I was convinced that the non-Serbian population of the municipality of Samac was being treated improperly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it was more than improperly. They were being treated -- they were being discriminated against on ethnic grounds, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, if there were elements for them to be detained in the sense that all those who possessed illegal weapons and took part in paramilitary formations and so on were to be locked up, there was no reason for them not to be subject to proper proceedings and for them to be subjected to beatings, branding, humiliation, and everything that these people went through. What I want to say is: If Mr. Todorovic, as the chief of the public security station and a member of the Crisis Staff, brought people in and charged them, then there was no reason for them to be mistreated and branded, which they were as a consequences of that. Nobody can justify that, in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just take you back to my question, and I'll demonstrate something. Your own evidence has been of those prisoners singing Chetnik songs. That was an act of humiliation and discrimination against non-Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And my question was: The people in detention, that's the non-Serbs, were being discriminated against on ethnic grounds by those who were detaining them, weren't they? That's as of the 26th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware of their -- of this discrimination against them on ethnic grounds - that's the prisoners in custody - as of that date, the 26th of April, 1992, weren't you? Based on a number of things: The singing of Chetnik songs, the ethnicity of the people in custody, the cursing of their balija mothers, and so on, and the insults directed towards them by their captors. All of those things convinced you, as at the 26th of April, 1992, that these prisoners were being discriminated against on ethnic grounds, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the 26th. I saw such scenes from the very outset. I think that such things happened even before, and I agree: In my view, the measures that were taken were improper, they were discriminatory, and they deserve condemnation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was Dr. Simic's participation in this process, as the president of the Crisis Staff, and your evidence is that the Crisis Staff were responsible, in your view, with Todorovic, for the takeover of the town with the paramilitaries, was it his participation in that process which you have just said was commenced before the 26th of April that led you to conclude in your book that he was a hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in my book which you keep referring to, I wrote only one sentence about Dr. Blagoje Simic, because I didn't want to deal with other people a lot, who are co-accused with me and brought here to The Hague along with me. Although to be quite honest, I never imagined I would be sitting in the dock together with Stevan Todorovic. But, well, that's human destiny. What I can say is - and that's my opinion - regardless of the fact that Mr. Todorovic, in the hierarchy, was connected to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, in my view, it was not unknown that we in the town of Samac had three or four rooms in which there were detainees, and I won't say that each and every member, including Mr. Blagoje Simic of the Executive Board or the Crisis Staff knew what went on there every night, but I think that the fact that people were detained and that there were many people there who were exposed to various kinds of suffering were known to them as a body. Therefore, from the viewpoint of political responsibility, I cannot separate the name of Dr. Blagoje Simic from the others, although I never saw or heard Mr. Blagoje Simic ordering Mr. Todorovic to do things like locking people up, raping them, beating them up, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was you believe that Dr. Simic had some responsibility for the takeover, on ethnic grounds, of Bosanski Samac. Your evidence was that Dr. Simic was the president of the Crisis Staff. Your evidence is that Mr. Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff, and he was responsible for the prisoners who were being subjected to the grossest forms of humiliation and discrimination. What I'm asking you is: Based upon what you know of Dr. Simic's participation in the entire process, as the leader -- the president of the Crisis Staff, when all this was occurring, is that one of the things that led you to conclude that he was a "hard-line politician and fiercely nationalistic"? Now, could you just concentrate on that part of the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you have asked this question I don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And Mr. Simo Zaric has been answering and explaining in his own way. Can we please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the removal of the prisoners from Brcko -- sorry, from the TO in Bosanski Samac to Brcko. Your evidence was a list was compiled, a list of people who were to be taken to Brcko. That was your evidence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes. The list that was compiled by the public security station commander, Mr. Stevan Cancarevic [as interpreted], and Mr. Mihajlo Topolovac, that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The list, of course -- I withdraw that. The list of prisoners to be taken was not the entirety of the prisoners being held in the TO, was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Later on I found out that not everybody had left. But at that time, I didn't know where people detained and who was detained. When I entered, I thought that they were all there, and that was the only facility. But other places, I never put my foot there, nor was I aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you went to the TO, it was dark, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dark. There was only a candle burning in the middle of that room, and in it - I found that out later - 56 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying there was only one candle lighting the entire room in which 56 people were held in?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That figure, 56, I heard from Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic when I went to see them the next day in Brcko, and then he told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the candle, what you saw. There was only one candle; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one candle, more or less, in the middle of the building, as said, which lit faces of people a little, but not enough to be able to discern who was sitting where and who were those people, so that it wasn't realistic to expect from me to register every single individual there in such a short time under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And based on that, you of course couldn't see what injuries had been inflicted on the 56 people who were in that room that you could only see by candlelight, could you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who were near the candle, one could see them, and that is why I told you what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The procedure was that someone read out names from a list, and those people came forward, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. The technique employed, I don't quite recollect, but I remember as they came and boarded the truck, that they helped one another and that Mr. Topolovac called out the names, one, two, three. I wasn't there all the time. At times I went out of the room and came back -- I mean I went out of the yard, because I was afraid that that other team might turn up and bring the whole election into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The people whose names were on the list were allowed onto the truck, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of people was read out. Now, following the methodology as I saw it, Mr. Topolovac was standing next to the truck. He was calling out people. What he was noting down, I did not follow that. So that that is what I could see at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: People whose names were read out were allowed onto the truck, but not everyone's name was read out, because there were some people left behind; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that they were left behind. It was later on that I learned that there were some people still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How later on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you told some people who were in the room that they were not coming with you, didn't you? At the time, not days later.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that to anyone. Where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You left behind a veterinarian; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... did he come with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Dr. Ante, Dr. Keljacic, he was there. I remember him. I remember Franjo Barukcic, Dragan Lukac, Sulejman Tihic. They all went off. Not a single name of those I mentioned stayed behind, nor did I know who stayed behind, nor did I see anybody stay there in that room, because I did not go back to I don't know -- check it later on. It never occurred to me. All I wanted to do was to have the operation finished, over, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told some people that they were political prisoners, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: None of the prisoners you transferred to Brcko that night were prisoners of war, were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What was your question? Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: None of the prisoners that you transferred to Brcko on the 26th of April into military custody were prisoners of war, none of them were armed combatants in uniform, were they, who had been captured in battle?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a legal question. All I know is that many of those who were there had weapons, and I know that some of them had come out into the street with arms that morning. If you think that that amounts to nothing, well, I don't know. I wouldn't go into that. However, it is a fact that a vast number of them had come into possession of illegal weapons through the paramilitary component. I have no doubts about that. But I did not go into their nature, whether they were prisoners of war, whether they were military captives. At that moment, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you're a long-time officer in the JNA, in the VRS. You know what a prisoner of war is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How would you -- I was some kind of an officer for a very short time before that. I was always in the civilian service. I worked in the public and state security. And as of January 1992, my official duty was assistant commander for security. And war broke out three months later. If you that I that is a long period of time, three months, then I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you know the difference between a civilian and an armed soldier, don't you, in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only those in uniforms need to be soldiers. It doesn't say anywhere if he's offering resistance and he's ready to fight, he need not wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: None of the people -- none of the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I don't think we should go into discussing whether these people were prisoners of war with Mr. Simo Zaric, because the evidence is there as to how they were arrested and by whom, and the circumstances are there. These are matters which can be matters of conclusion after analysing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I'll move on from that. You said you told some people that they were political prisoners. They were, of course, Muslim and Croat political prisoners, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I answered that question when Mr. Lukac, whom I had not properly recognised because he was wearing a beard, not far from that candle, he asked me and said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... answer yes. The question was very simple.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But I have to explain why I said that, Mr. Prosecutor. I didn't say it because I thought that political prisoners should be detained and beaten there. If you want to charge me with something like that and allow me to defend myself to say that it's not true, that it's a fabrication, that it's a lie, whatever, it has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zaric, I'll just take you back. These people you described as political prisoners were Muslims and Croats, weren't they? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Political prisoners, as far as you're concerned, and you have had a long history in intelligence, are people detained for their political views, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basically that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your view was that these particular people, who were Muslims and Croats, were being detained for their political views, that is, they were being discriminated against because of their political views as Muslims and Croats, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point of time, I thought that because of their political positions that I upheld before the detention, thinking that the democratic tone advocated by people in the Serb Democratic Party would prevail, that it would be stronger than the fact that those people were in prison. Because I could not see why should a politician be pushed into prison and placed at a disadvantage. And that is why I said it.
