I said I think that with your politicians things will soon be over and you'll be released in due time. I even made an optimistic assessment as for other people, and those words I thought that the conscience of our people are those who decided on the politics, on the fate of democracy that one of them would say why should Sulejman Tihic be in prison now if yesterday he was a political partner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question was quite simple. Your view was that these particular people you described as political prisoners, who were Muslims and Croats, were being discriminated against because of their political views as Muslims and Croats, wasn't it? You can answer that quite simply. Was that your view?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the political positions they had held beforehand, so I didn't know much about their political views. The fact that somebody was a member of the HDZ or the SDA meant nothing to me. I merely knew that they held certain positions, that they were either members of the Main Board of the HDZ or the SDA. But I don't know whether that is a criterion to send somebody to prison. Not to my mind, and that is why I said what I said then, and I still think the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not a legitimate criteria to send people to prison, was it, but that's what happened, that's what you saw, people being detained who were Muslims and Croats, detained because of their ethnicity and political view. That's what you saw, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that, and it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those people weren't people you wanted to further interrogate, were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The people you described as political prisoners were not the people you wanted to interrogate further about illegal arming and so on, were they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of illegal arming is one thing, and somebody -- the views of somebody who held an important political position is another matter. So if I interrogated somebody in relation to illegal arming is one matter, and policy and these things I didn't really go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Some of the people who you were removing to Brcko you wished to interrogate further in relation to the arming, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained how these three interviews with Mr. Nalic and brothers Bicic came about, and how --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please just answer for once the question. The question this time was: Some of the people who you were removing to Brcko you wished to further interrogate in relation to the illegal arming, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but it just so happened, so I did conduct those interviews, and I am not denying that I did that. There is nothing doubtful about that. And the way how I did it and how I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That is, the people you moved from civilian or paramilitary custody on the 26th of April into military custody you interrogated some of them further into relation to the arming, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that was one of the reasons why you moved them into military custody, apart from the humanitarian reasons, it enabled you to interrogate them further in the sanctity of JNA facilities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not my intention. The conversation was spontaneous. I went one day to see them, and after that I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a long-time employee of the ministry of internal affairs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were very familiar with the laws on internal affairs, weren't you, and of course as you would have been as a former police chief?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew about -- I knew a decent amount of things to be able to perform that duty. I mean, the chief of a public security station needed to understand certain things, and I believe I was knowledgeable about that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You needed to be intimately familiar with the laws under which you were operating the public security station, didn't you, Mr. Zaric? There's a short answer to that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have to, but I did my best to know it. At the time when I was the chief of the public security station, then that office was more of a political nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were employed by the ministry of internal affairs, the MUP, in 1990 and 1991. You were familiar with the 1990 law on internal affairs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the state security, I can talk about that, and at that time I worked for the state security. If you want to learn something about that, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm simply talking about the law on internal affairs. As an employee and a senior one, you were aware of and familiar with the 1990 law on internal affairs, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What had to do with the state security service, yes. I didn't work for the public security to be aware of the law of the interior, which has to do with that part. But from a period in my life between 1975 to 1979, when I was SUP chief, I was aware of the basic concept underlying the law on the internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska established its own law on internal affairs in February 1992, a month after the declaration or the proclamation of the Republika Srpska, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it. I mean, I heard that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard that information. That was during the period when you were working in the reserve for the SJB, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in the reserve of the state security service. I was never in the reserve of the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. That was my error. The SDB. You were in the SDB reserve at the time of the adoption of the Republika Srpska law on internal affairs in February 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the field of my work had to do with the state security of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not some kind of Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may not have, but at the time when you were in the SDB reserve in January and February 1992, you were aware of the divisions within the Bosnian government MUP, weren't you, on political grounds?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, of course. That is why I was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware that the Republika Srpska established 13 ministries in February 1992, including a ministry of internal affairs, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I don't know how many ministries they established, but no doubt that one of the more important ministries was the one of the interior, and I believe that the Ministry of the Interior, at that time, in that government, became an official ministry, but that there were 13 of them, I really don't know, because I never went into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware at the time of the establishment of the Serbian -- of the Serb MUP that Bosnian government MUP officials were leaving it to work for the Serbian MUP, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only insofar as it had to do with the reserve part of the police, as far as I know. But Serbs were not the only ones to do it. That's quite true. That was the reserve police. And the active-duty police in Samac remained part of the public security station to the very last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were also aware that the law proclaimed on internal affairs by the Republika Srpska in February 1992 was almost identical to that of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 1990 law, weren't you? Because that was the law in force in the Republika Srpska thereafter.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I never read it. But I do not think that those people could do something -- special, because the law on the internal -- the laws on internal affairs across former Yugoslavia are very similar. So that I think that the law on internal affairs of Republika Srpska was very much like the law applicable at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, I am guessing. I never read it, but I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The old law divided Bosnia into nine CSBs or security centre reasons. The new law divided them into five. Doboj was the centre for the SAO of northern Bosnia, wasn't it? That is, the Bosanski Samac police -- security -- sorry, public security station reported to Doboj, didn't it, under the new law?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this structure under the new law. Before that, the Security Services Centre in Doboj covered 11 municipalities, including the municipality of Samac. I know that because I had worked in that region for a long time, as the chief, and then in the state security sector. But how was it done in this new organisational layout in Republika Srpska, how did those authorities did it, well, I didn't do my homework in that regard properly, so I'd rather not say something. If I knew it, I'd tell you openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska ministry of internal affairs was divided just like the Bosnian one, old one, into a public security service and a national security service, although there had been a name change from state security service, that's SDB, to national security service, SNB; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that later on, because - I'll be brief - when they said they were appointing me chief for national security, the term was strange to me. So I asked if it was something like what I had done in the state security service, and then they explained that, yes, it was similar to that. Later on I heard that the national security service had been established as part of the sector in the ministry, and yes, you are correct. The other sector had to do with public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The role of the state security division under the new law was to gather information aimed at detecting and preventing activities of individuals, groups, and organisations who conspire to violate the constitutional order and state security of the Republika Srpska. That's consistent with your understanding of the role of the new state security division, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said, that's what I did in the state security service of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If that's what it says, then they simply copied it. That was exactly how information was gathered. I never gathered any information for the national security service of Republika Srpska. But the job description was as you have read it out, as far as I can remember, when I worked in the state security service of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And state security for the Republika Srpska MUP in the war was divided into three lines: Intelligence, counter-intelligence, and technical operations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't get an interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The state security for the Republika Srpska MUP in the war was divided into three lines - intelligence, counter-intelligence, and technical operations - wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, because I didn't work in that sector. I can only guess. But previously in the state security service of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was an intelligence part and a counter-intelligence part. Those were segments that the service dealt with. And when my counsel, Pisarevic, was examining me, I think I explained this in detail. I don't know to what extent I can talk about the new organisation, because I didn't have much to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One of the things the new law provided was that the CSBs and SJBs were to cease cooperating with the Bosnian ministry of internal affairs and henceforth cooperate only with the Republika Srpska one. That's from the 28th of February onwards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was from that point in time. I really couldn't say. But I know that when the war broke out and when there was complete differentiation, I can only assume that in this entity of Republika Srpska, things were done as you say, and that later on new centres -- new public security centres and stations were set up and that the service was set up a little bit differently in technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The new MUP and its employees was well and truly established by the date of the takeover in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that that's how it should have been, but I'm not sure how long it took. In view of the environment we were in, for Mr. Stevan Todorovic, as chief of the public security station, to contact his superiors in Doboj or the Ministry of the Interior in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He was, of course, appointed on the 28th of March, 1992. He was in place weeks before the takeover, as the head of the Serbian municipality's public security station. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read the document that was before you, I can assume that's how it was, but I know that no Serbian public security station was operating in public or was talked about. I really don't know. If Mr. Todorovic did something illegally, and he evidently did something that was not done in public, then that's a different story. But what was stated in public was that there was a public security station whose chief was Dragan Lukac. That's what was known before the conflict broke out on the 16th and 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you knew, before the conflict, that Mr. Todorovic had been appointed by the Samac Serbian municipality, or Municipal Assembly, as its chief of the public security station, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard people talking about that behind the scenes, and it seems strange to me, but it was never actually officially announced in public, until, of course, when I arrived here, I saw these Official Gazettes, and then I saw that they had had sessions and made appointments, and now I can see what a poor intelligence officer I was when I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... information that Mr. Todorovic has been appointed. Mr. Zaric used the word: It was funny. It sounds funny to me. He didn't say strange to me. He said funny. Because he was referring to Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Funny, strange. It doesn't alter the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The SNB, that's the new state security service, cooperated and worked closely with military intelligence during the war, didn't it? You're aware of that because of your work in military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had an opportunity to talk to anyone from the national security service as assistant commander of the 4th Detachment for security, which was in place until the 12th of May, when there was a transformation in the army of Republika Srpska. Whether the national security service cooperated with the Military Intelligence Service through the war, I don't know, but I assume they did, because it would have been normal for them to do so. However, I was not involved with that, so I have no first-hand knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And until the official withdrawal of the JNA on the 12th of May, 1992, the Republika Srpska MUP were the only armed forces which were exclusively under the control of the Republika Srpska leadership, weren't they? Because at that stage, the TOs were under JNA control.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this fact because it's something I don't know. If I refer to what was happening in Samac, the Serbian public security service, which would be headed, after the 16th, by Mr. Stevan Todorovic, this was something that was not felt in public opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer. I was there. But as for their activities, I knew only that members of the reserve police force in Samac received the suggestion that they should not be in the regular police force, and some of them left. And the police force in Samac remained a part of the public security service until the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence was of the public security station having a room which the SDB used and which you used when you were in the reserve between the 1st of October, 1991 and the beginning of April -- and sorry, mid-April 1992. Did you have the key to that room?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key was with the chief for defence preparations. His name was Boro Cvijanovic. And he was an active employee of the SDB in Modrica. And he had a deputy, Stanko Dujkovic, in Samac, who had the key to that room. And the service used that room not from that period but for years the SDB had had this room at its disposal for meetings of the reserve SDB department.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The SDB had an office in the public security station, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you used that -- I'm sorry, the SNB, that's the successor, continued to use that room after the takeover, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. No, that's got nothing to do with it. It's really got nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The SNB had an office in the state security -- sorry, the public security office after the takeover, didn't it? It worked from there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That office was broken into and it was never again used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did the SNB work from after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't exist. It did not exist after the outbreak of hostilities, the SDB in Bosanski Samac, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I said SNB. That's the state security service. I'm sorry, the national security service. Where did it work from in Bosanski Samac after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no service, no office. There were no employees. There was nothing. I don't know where you found this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was paying you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. I did not receive any salary at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was paying you when you were in the army on the command staff of the 2nd Posavina Brigade? Who was paying your salary?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received our salaries through the command, and I will not repeat. It was so negligent that there's no need to talk about it. Instead of money we were given goods and that's how we survived and we ate from the mess where the soldiers ate, the privates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you swear an oath of loyalty to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took an oath to the JNA once in my life, and after that never again to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were appointed the chief of national security by the Crisis Staff on the 29th of April, 1992. That was at the same time that Stevan Todorovic was the chief of public security, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And those were the dual roles envisaged by the Republika Srpska law on internal affairs, published in February 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you're not correct. The public security service is organised according to municipalities. The national security service has quite different methods of work. It's always organised according to regions. And there was no national security employee attached to a municipality. They were organised by regions, small regions, large regions, and finally the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your capacity as chief of national security, you questioned people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were authorised to collect information and to question people, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this had to do with my job as assistant commander for security in the 4th Detachment, and later the 5th Infantry Battalion. Never did I do any job for the national security service, nor did I ever submit any report to anyone in this capacity. I have been repeating this like a parrot for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the statement you made to the Prosecutor on the 2nd of June, 1998. That's P142 ter. I want you to turn, please, to page 89 and 90.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found page 88. Did you see 88?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Page 89, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 89. Yes, here it is before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You'll see, about a third of the way down the page, it says: "John" - that's the lawyer from the OTP - "Sir, would you please tell me what your responsibilities as this new -- under your new position of chief of national security was." Your answer was: "Since I was earlier chief of the state security, when the new authorities were formed in the area of Republika Srpska, and when Republika Srpska was proclaimed within Bosnia and Herzegovina, that service, instead of being called the state security service was called national security -- sorry, the service for national security." The lawyer -- I've read that correctly, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The lawyer says: "Okay, Mr. Zaric. I understand all that. My question was: What were your responsibilities? Please answer my questions as briefly as you can!" Your answer was, over the page at page 90: "As chief of national security, considering the fact that it was war is a question of collecting further data relevant for the defence of the town in which I was. The facts relevant to the defence of the territory which was under the command of the army of Republika Srpska. I had no special authority other than collecting such data which is what I did in conducting certain questionings, acquired certain data and knowledge which pointed to the fact that the other side prepared similar things such as the SDS party. But with no activity of my own or by no activity of my own as chief of national security did I bring any personal hurt or bring anyone into a situation, and when the first time I wanted to go and coordinate the work of the service at the session of the Crisis Staff which I attended, I was immediately demoted. It was the same moment when the JNA left Samac on the 19th." Now, Mr. Zaric, I read that correctly, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. When you were conducting interviews in the SUP, after the 29th of April, 1992, and into May 1992, you were doing so when you were the chief of national security for the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: According to your answer here at page 90 or 91 on the copy you have, you said: "I had no special authority other than collecting such data which is what I did in conducting certain questionings, acquired certain data and knowledge which appointed to the fact that the other side prepared similar things such as the SDS party." Now, Mr. Zaric, you've told us at length about interrogating or questioning people in relation to illegal arming. What you're referring to there is what the other side did. You're referring to the flip side of the SDS arming, the arming by the other parties, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were arming too, the other side, in a similar way. That's what I said. But what you are now trying to explain, when I said that I was the chief of the national security service, I said the task was to gather information important for the defence of the town, and I was on the territory that the army of Republika Srpska was in charge of. But nowhere does it say that I reported to the Crisis Staff. It was in the army that I carried out questionings, on orders from my commander, and held a few interviews with a few people, and did that quite professionally, quite properly, and completed the task that had been assigned to me, according to my orders. I had nothing to do with the national security for the Crisis Staff. I only received a decision and at the next session I was replaced. And I have already explained how this came about. Because I challenged the legality of this decision and that they could appoint me. This is in my interview. But either you don't want to find it or you're not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. It's just not what it says, Mr. Zaric. It says that you conducted certain questionings, acquired certain data and knowledge, pointing to the fact that the other side prepared similar things such as the SDS party. You've said you did those things in your capacity as the chief of national security. That's what it says, plainly and simply, isn't it, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what it says. That's not how I interpret it. I say that I was working under the leadership of the army of Republika Srpska, and that was why I conducted interviews. I did nothing in the capacity of chief of national security, and I did not imperil anyone or bring them into a situation that was not good. If the service existed, it had to have a head and tail. I said that this should be done properly, in consultation with Pale. And I was replaced. They simply gave me a document which I did not agree with. I worked only for the army of Republika Srpska, under orders from my commander, and I did nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If that's the case, how -- can you perhaps tell us how the Crisis Staff could demote you, if you were only working for the VRS, after you had gone there to try to coordinate the work of this national security service to which they had appointed you? How could the Crisis Staff demote you if you're working exclusively for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not making use of me. They didn't replace me. I never received any decision or anything else. It was their wish to say in public that they wanted to dismiss me so that Simo was no longer a member of national security, and I was not interested in that. I didn't care. Because I never became a member of the national security service, because only the minister of the interior can issue such a document, not the Crisis Staff in Samac. And the fact that they dismissed me at such a session in such a vulgar way, that's another matter. It has to do with relations between me and some people in the Crisis Staff. And that is why I used that word, saying that they had dismissed me. That is how it ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the Trial Chamber expects you to complete your cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Your Honours. I really am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because you were allowed two days, and we had started on Thursday, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I want to take you to the circumstances of your appointment as chief of national security. Can you please turn to your book, at page 251. You can see a photograph caption, there's photos, and underneath there, there's a 2. Maybe it's the next page over. It starts: "Towards the end of April, they asked me to come to the Crisis Staff." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What it says is: "Towards the end of April, they asked me to come to the Crisis Staff, with no spontaneity at all, the president, Blagoje Simic, told me I had been appointed chief of national security. He explained that I was well-qualified for the position and that it was `a sign both of immense trust and of the need to coordinate in a new and different manner the activities of the Serb state, the JNA, and the Serb army, which must be created, for without it there could be no Serb state.' I was taken aback. Where did that come from? I could not accept it even if I had wanted to, for I had a post and duties in the JNA, where my tasks were similar. Simic told me not to worry, for that had already been taken care of. He said he had talked with Nikolic, who had nothing against it. He went on to explain that it was a good solution, because some things in connection with the 4th Detachment inevitably had to be more clearly defined. The security structure was becoming more fully rounded and the JNA's prerogatives were reduced. We have all been mobilised anyway. We are all soldiers in our own way. The defence is single and indivisible, and so it does not matter under whose command you are. "You cannot counter a clever and cunning explanation with disbelief, and it was not for me to say that I refused or that it was out of the question, especially if Nikolic had given his approval. It is not like him not to have at least given me a hint of this, nor do I believe that they would lie so outrageously either. Most likely, things are `somewhere in between,' but whatever the case may be, I have no choice but to accept my appointment. As soon as I tried to define my new position, it became clear to me that I was out in the cold without a clue, with nothing to hold on to, in fact. Nikolic told me he had discussed things with the Crisis Staff but that their request had been neither concrete nor urgent. They had stopped by in passing and raised a couple of issues quite casually, including that of the creation of a Serb army and how to avoid overlap and misunderstandings with the JNA. In this context, they also mentioned the inevitable transformation of the 4th Detachment into an integral part of the Serb army. Nikolic told them he was not competent to deal with such issues, so he forwarded everything to his Superior Command and could not talk to me about it until an answer arrived. He concluded by saying, `No matter how these things are set up, it's a good thing that you'll be in the midst of things. It doesn't matter. You can be both here and there until that gets off the ground. You don't have a choice. Just make sure that you don't fall out with him first thing. Adapt, train them to listen to you. There's no other way with them.'" Now, I read that correctly, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that quite clearly shows that Nikolic approved of your appointment as chief of national security while you were simultaneously working in intelligence for him. He approved you working for the Crisis Staff and for him at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a very short conversation on that subject, and he said that they had talked to him in passing and that that was all. But my most important conclusion was that in spite of everything, I refused to do it, and that is the gist of it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you now saying that you refused to be the chief of national security, you refused to accept the appointment and did not take it up? Is that what you're now saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. That's what I'm saying. The moment I started discussion with them to tell them what I meant by national security and what I was asking for. And on page 253, it says there that's how we started our marriage. It didn't take longer -- it didn't last longer than 20 days. We have not started a job or that what we started, we never finished. They did not allow me as if some ill suited bride. They wouldn't even let me to go to my people, in quotation marks, to Pale, to Zoran Skipinja [phoen], who as far as I can remember was then an honest man who was about to set up the Serb security service. And that is the conclusion that one can draw from that whole sequence. So I did not accept it all, and when I wanted to go, they wouldn't let me. So the marriage between us was dissolved. Simo Zaric went back to his old job, the one that I had been doing until that time in the detachment. And that's all there is to it, Mr. Prosecutor, and that is the only truth that I stand by. There is no other truth. And I apologise. Perhaps it's not for me to say, but, Your Honours, that is why my book is of any value, only if it is read from one cover to the other. Otherwise, taking out excerpts, taking it out, I mean, it loses its value and one misses the right conclusion what its purpose was. I don't know how it will be treated in the end, but this was just a comment I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric. We note that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But in the context of your statement, P142 ter, at page 91, where you said you conducted certain questionings and acquired certain data and knowledge, I just want to ask you: What were the questionings you conducted and the data you acquired when you were the chief of national security, as you've indicated in your statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't working as chief of national security, and don't put these words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you go to your book, at about page 196.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's below the photograph, referring to a meeting with Nikolic at Pelagicevo in April 1992, before the takeover. The first paragraph I want to refer you to says: "Going back to a very concrete issue ..." Page 197.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't get you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: About page 197, the paragraph starts: "Going back to a very concrete issue which had brought us to Pelagicevo in the first place, we wanted to know what kind of attitude to assume towards Izetbegovic's TO staff, as we called it. Nikolic was quite firm. We are under JNA command and remain directly subordinated to him."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which page did you say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Fine. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What you're referring to there is a security briefing by Colonel Nikolic at command headquarters in Pelagicevo, after the paramilitaries arrived and before the takeover. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what kind of conclusion you are drawing from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you: Is that the particular meeting we're referring to, a briefing, security briefing, by Nikolic, at command headquarters in Pelagicevo in April, before the takeover and after the arrival of the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, but then when you read a book, you must start two or three pages ahead and say that there were a few officers who voiced their views and there were all sorts of comments. And you take out a sentence and want me to say yes, and I really cannot answer in this way, because you are trying to put together your own construct and I'm really unable to do it that way. Because if I'm to know what meeting you're talking about, I need to write two pages before and two pages after. How else can I know what meeting it is and that it is a meeting, as you put it, before the arrival of volunteers, and I don't know what did you say. I'd need time to concentrate, to read it, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would be quicker to read the book to satisfy yourself that that's the meeting I'm referring to. If you go back a couple of pages and just satisfy yourself that that's the meeting I'm referring to. I'm just trying to place it in context, that's all.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is my difficulty. You put it in a context and I need time to concentrate. Yes, right. Now I don't know what it is you want. I've read a little, but I really don't know what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you: Am I correct in saying it was the security briefing by Nikolic at command headquarters in Pelagicevo, between the arrival of the paramilitaries and the takeover? If I'm not correct, please correct me as to which meeting it was. It's your book, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I don't know why you used the word briefing. It could have been a meeting. And there is talk here about this meeting and what another officer, Nikolic said. He voiced some of his thoughts and then we addressed questions concerning Territorial Defence and some thoughts. Because throughout here on this page, 197, I'm trying to paraphrase the words of an officer who had made a specific comment, and the whole page deals with that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've asked you three times. I'm just asking you whether that was when the meeting took place, not this other stuff. It's your book. You wrote a book. You referred to a meeting. I'm just asking you if I'm correct in saying that's when the meeting occurred. I'm giving you the time to check your book, the pages before, to find out. Please do so and just tell me whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting mentioned here addresses the topic which was mentioned, the Territorial Defence, and that is what we talked about. If you mean that, that meeting took place and you could see what I had to say about it, in the book, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am attempting to find out when the meeting took place. It cannot be that difficult, surely. He wrote the book. He's got it in front of him. He's just deliberately, in my submission, not answering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be clearer if you -- I'm not sure whether you pointed out the actual passages referring to the meeting discussed in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have. I have. It's that page. And he says he needs to look at the pages immediately prior to find out which meeting I'm referring to. I just want to find out whether it was in that time frame. All I'm interested in at the moment is time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a meeting which took place before that meeting in the neighbourhood locality centre. That is what you mean, the one that took place in the neighbourhood community centre in the evening of the 16th, if that is the meeting that you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zaric, I take you to what you say there, page 197, below the first paragraph I referred you to, the next one: "Then he informed us briefly about the security outlook, he being Nikolic. He said that the Serbs would certainly not just sit and wait for Alija to establish his own Territorial Defence and use it as the basis for building an army. They would use every opportunity to throw a spanner in the works. In many areas, the SDS -- I'm sorry, the SDS is making quick progress in mobilising and organising the Serb masses, for they have no choice left. They have been virtually outlawed and have no reason to wait. That is why they are making energetic moves. As to what kind of moves the local Serbs would `make,' that remains to be seen. "I dared not ask him too directly what we could expect here, or even more directly how the Serb question would be resolved in Posavina, but approach the subject in a round about way. I said, meaning I, Simo Zaric, said: Haven't Zvornik, Bijeljina, and Vlasenica been a lesson to Izetbegovic not to oppose the Serbs? And which municipality is next?" I read that correctly to you, didn't I, Mr. Zaric? That's page 141 of the English.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's page 198. It's not 197. It's 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 198, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, and I've been... Yes. I've found it, on page 198. And you gave me the wrong page, and therefore I couldn't concentrate and find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought when I said: Have you got that paragraph, that you did in fact have it. Can you just read it to yourself and just confirm that I've read it out correctly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that is on page 198. That is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraph which I just read to you, commencing at: "Then he informed us briefly about the security outlook..." And the next paragraph: "I dared not ask him too directly what we could expect here. Haven't Zvornik, Bijeljina, and Vlasenica been a lesson to Izetbegovic not to oppose the Serbs? And which municipality is next?" I read that out correctly, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you did. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to turn to about page 226. Now, there's a photograph -- go several pages over until you come to a 2, which is the second section.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just above the 2, three paragraphs up, you'll see one that begins: "Nikolic then warned Simic again..." And just to find the context, that is Nikolic talking to Dr. Simic about the release or after the release of the members of the 4th Detachment from custody.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. What you say, that Nikolic said when you were there to Simic was: "Nikolic" -- it's at page 166 of the English. "Nikolic then warns Simic again and mentioned Todorovic. 2. `You'll have to pay for anything these volunteers might do. You have no experience with such scum. They will get out of hand and you'll have terrible trouble with them. There have been dozens of such cases in Croatia. You've got to put them under your command and control. If you can't do that, ask me for help, but ask officially. I give you my word. I'll send them packing to where they've come from. But I don't want to be seen as interfering in civilian matters without the consent of the authorities.'" I've read that correctly, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, that occurred, I think, was it on the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I guess so. I guess it could have been the date when Antic and I interceded because of what happened. They arrested members of the 4th Detachment and we were at the commander's when he called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, that was a clear warning from Nikolic to Simic as to the danger that these paramilitaries or volunteers posed to people in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it also shows that both you and Nikolic appreciated, as at least of the 18th of April, how dangerous these people were, especially when you go back to the context of the earlier quote about what they had done in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Vlasenica, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic was certainly in a better position than me to know this. Excuse me. I gave my assessment on the basis of what I was able to read in the media, and that's why I made a certain comment. How dangerous they already were on the 18th, this was an assessment put forward by Mr. Nikolic in the context that's to be found in the book. Because even before Samac was taken, some moves they made on the territory of the municipality indicated that these were very dangerous people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to go over the page, where it says 2. You see the division 2? The first, second, third -- fourth paragraph, starting: "If Simic and Todorovic..." Have you found that? Four paragraphs in from 2.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And what you say there, this is at page 167 of the English, what page is it in the B/C/S? Can you just tell us the page number? Is it page 227 or 228?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 231 in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. What it says is: "If Simic and Todorovic have in a way let me know that `my days are over after all' I do not think that this was really meant personally. What they wanted to tell me in their own way was that from now on, Croats, Muslims, and even Yugoslavs would be treated differently. This had been immediately clear to the Muslims and Croats, for what could they have expected from the new authorities, since their own people had been preparing to persecute and slaughter Serbs an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth?" I've read that correctly, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from that, it's clear that it was your belief, in April 1992, that Muslims and Croats could have been expected -- could have been expecting persecution from the new Serb authorities in Bosanski Samac because that's exactly what they had been preparing to do to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the assessment I put forward. Although I have to admit when I go back to the beginning of the page and see what event is referred to here, when I was very angry, due to arrests of volunteers, and I had a verbal exchange with Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Simic, and they were very cynical in their replies to me. So that this passage which refers to Simic and Todorovic, I think it refers to Milan Simic and not to Blagoje Simic, because it was they I had a vehement quarrel with in this connection, and they said that my time was past. These were the words they often used. I never had such a vehement quarrel with Blagoje, so I think that this quotation does not -- is not quite correct and I wouldn't want to have this associated with Mr. Blagoje Simic, if this is not it. But that was my view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we can clarify a bit this answer, because here it says: "Due to arrests of volunteers," and frankly, I'm not quite sure what Mr. Zaric was referring. Maybe Mr. Re can clarify. Arrests of certain people in Bosanski Samac done by the volunteers or his arrest or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Zaric can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were referring, Mr. Zaric, to the arrest of members of the 4th Detachment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the fact that Todorovic and Simic interceded to have them released from - that's Blagoje Simic - interceded to have them released from custody. That's what you were referring to, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikolic interceded through them to have them released, and I had direct contacts in the agricultural complex. When we had a vehement quarrel about this and these words to discredit me saying that my time was passed were spoken by Mr. Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic. Commander Nikolic had a telephone conversation with Simic and Todorovic in order to have the members of the 4th Detachment released from detention, those who were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Re. I think the confusion to which Mr. Lazarevic was referring is on page 72, line 16 -- no, 15. The expression -- or let's start: "When I was very angry due to the arrests of volunteers." Did it mean arrest -- did you mean, Mr. Zaric, arrest of volunteers or the arrests carried out by the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was angry because members of the 4th Detachment were arrested by the volunteers and by members of the police force. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But several pages earlier, Mr. Zaric, at page 226, if you just look for the words -- a paragraph about three paragraphs past the photographs, maybe 227, it starts: "At Hranaprodukt, where they had their headquarters ..." It will be past page 226. It's maybe 227.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 228, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 228.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's 164 in the English, and it says: "At Hranaprodukt, where they had their headquarters, I found Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic and some of their collaborators. I told them what had happened, trying to keep all emotion out of the story, not to let them know how I felt but to leave the impression of someone who was not afraid, who will not crawl into a hole, to show that I was not just anyone. This could not be brushed aside just like that. What they said to me by way of explanation was neither condemnation nor excuse." And then you go on to a conversation that you had between Todorovic and Blagoje Simic. And if you read then, you see it's after that that Nikolic -- that you went to see Antic and Nikolic. Nikolic picked up the phone and called Simic, that's Blagoje Simic, and had that conversation we referred to a few moments ago, where he said: "You'll have to pay for anything these volunteers do. You have no experience with such scum." Clearly what you're referring to, in the context of this, that's the arrest of the members of the 4th Detachment, is the conversation between Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say -- it says Hranaprodukt here by mistake. There was never a Crisis Staff headquarters in Hranaprodukt. It was in the agricultural complex. And there is a typing error here. The fact that I mentioned Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic with some associates of theirs, while Mr. Milan Simic was among those associates, and when the quarrel broke out, my quarrel was with Mr. Milan Simic and Blagoje [as interpreted]. Commander Nikolic, when Antic and I went to see him, as far as we could see, had a telephone conversation with Todorovic and Blagoje Simic, and he told them that the members of the 4th Detachment should be released from detention. And then I went and carried out that task. I had a vehement quarrel with Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Stevan Todorovic about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it was a slip of the tongue or something, but because here in -- we have two sentences with some contradictory statements. First it says: "My quarrel was with Mr. Milan Simic and Blagoje." And on the last sentence, it says: "I had a quarrel with Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Stevan Todorovic about this." So maybe my colleague could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I think, if I may intervene, I think it's quite obvious that on page 75, line 9, the last word should not be Blagoje, but Todorovic. It doesn't need any clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You've seen the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, by July 1992, you were no longer chief of national security and you were back in the military, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this time, I was assistant commander for security of the 5th Infantry Battalion, up to the 20th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was your successor as chief of national security at the public security station after you left the position in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that quite late in the autumn, I think, a gentleman called Ratko Mihajlovic was appointed. But I wasn't interested in that area any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In July 1992, the Crisis Staff appointed you to the position of deputy or assistant to the president of the war council for security matters of Odzak municipality, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed assistant president of the civilian military council in Odzak. I was not the deputy. And it was only for security matters. That's what was said at the very outset, when I started off in the direction of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the Crisis Staff's or War Presidency's powers to appoint you to that particular position, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't appoint me. A meeting was held in the president's office, and I never received a document. I had my wartime assignment for that month, and it was a purely military assignment, at the military command, because everything I did in Odzak I did for the military security and collected information for the military security, except for the first few days when I participated in the taking of the inventory of property, which I mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the position of deputy to the president of the war council for security matters in Odzak municipality, you reported directly to the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, your lawyers filed with the Prosecution a document called joint statement of admissions by the parties in matters which are not in dispute. It was filed on the 27th of April, 2001, several months before this trial began. And I take Your Honours to paragraph 94, which is the paragraph about you, Mr. Zaric. And it says: "On 29th of April, 1992, Simo Zaric was appointed chief of national security service for Bosanski Samac by the Serb Crisis Staff." It goes on: "After the Serb takeover of Odzak in July 1992, Simo Zaric, that's you, was appointed by the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff to be the deputy to the president of the war council for security matters of the Odzak municipality. In the position of deputy to the president of the war council for security matters of the Odzak municipality, Simo Zaric reported directly to the Serb Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac." It goes on: "On the 1st of September, 1992, Simo Zaric was appointed `assistant commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade for morale and information' of the Bosnian Serb army. Simo Zaric remained member of the Bosnian Serb army until 1995." Now, Mr. Zaric, that's a document your lawyers agreed to before the trial commenced, which states clearly that you were appointed by the Crisis Staff to that position, and in that position you reported directly to the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac. You instructed your lawyers that that was the case, didn't you? What I mean by that is you told your lawyers that you were appointed to that position by the Crisis Staff, and in that position you reported to the Crisis Staff. That's what you told your lawyers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know. This is a legal matter. And let my Defence respond to it as they think they should. But I want to tell Their Honours: When a request was made that a certain number of people from Odzak municipality who had been born there should go to the area of Odzak and set up a civilian military council --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll come to that. I'm asking you only about this document at the moment. This document was prepared. All the lawyers prepared it. They agreed on the facts. What I'm asking you is: Did you tell your lawyer, who approved this document, that you had been, A, appointed by the Crisis Staff to the position I named; and B, reported to the Crisis Staff? Or have your lawyers all got this horribly wrong? Or a third alternative: Have you changed your version? You told them that and now you've changed it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I understood that I was appointed by the Crisis Staff because this happened in the office of the president of the Crisis Staff. I did not get any document. And there was never mention of a deputy, but only the assistant of the president of the civilian military council. The word "war" was not used. And when a proposal was put forward that I should be the president of that civilian council, then it was Savo Popovic who was to be appointed to that place, because he was a member of the staff. I went to Odzak, and as someone who was in charge of security, who had been assigned that task by the military administration, I received my instructions from their security officer for the military administration as to what I should do, what information I should collect, and report to him. That's what I did for a month. Not a single report of any kind did I submit to the Crisis Staff, and that is why I do not consider myself to have been responsible in any way to the Crisis Staff. I was responsible and reported to the security officer of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you have any explanation for the fact that the -- the facts your lawyers agreed to were that the Crisis Staff -- sorry, A, the Crisis Staff appointed you; and B, you reported to them. Do you have any explanation for why your lawyers approved those two facts going into this document? That's all I'm asking you. Please just concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they accepted the fact because I said it was in the office of the Crisis Staff, and because I said how I had been sent there, then I cannot change that. That's how I experienced it. But what I did in Odzak during that month, intelligence work, security work, collecting information, you were able to see the three notes I drew up after interviewing a certain number of people, and of course there were many other notes that the court, this court, was not interested in. But I did not report to the Crisis Staff, and everything that had to be done for the civilian military council in Odzak, the Crisis Staff of the Executive Board in Bosanski Samac had to do with Savo Popovic, who was the president of that council and the official authorities in Samac. And I had no personal relations or official relations with the Crisis Staff in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, rather than belabour the question, I'll move on to another one, but I just note that you haven't answered the second part, which is how the part about your reporting back to the Crisis Staff came to be in the document. But as you choose not to answer it, I will move on. You were acting under orders of the Crisis Staff when you were the deputy or assistant for war or civilian matters for security, however it's termed, in Odzak, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I had been responsible to them, I would have reported to them. I would have had to submit a report. I would have had to do something in relation to the Crisis Staff. What did I do in relation to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because if you were under orders from the Crisis Staff, that would entail reporting back to them, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been, yes, then I would have had to report to them. But since I didn't, I didn't. I reported to the security officer, Gojko Mackic, who was the security officer of the military administration in the entire area of responsibility of Odzak, where I worked and collected information. And this security information was never given to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The short answer to that would have been yes, wouldn't it? Now, let's move on. Being under orders from the Crisis Staff would entail reporting back to them and doing their work for them in Odzak, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you're getting at. I did not work based on the orders of the Crisis Staff. You are trying to press it upon me, but I'm saying I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm getting to what you said at page 136 of P142 ter, Mr. Zaric. Please turn to that. That's the interview with the Prosecutor on the 3rd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it's time for us to break off.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll continue this afternoon I think in courtroom 1. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 2.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I was taking you to before the break, Mr. Zaric, was a quote -- I'm sorry, was your answer at page 136 of P142. Maybe if you read the page before, it may help to put it into context. The page -- do you have it there, that's page 135 and 136 of P142 ter, which is the interview on the 3rd of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Which page did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The page 135 and 136 of P142 ter, the interview of the 3rd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can take you to page 135, where it starts, a third of the way through, the lawyer, John, Mr. Misilic [phoen], says: "No. But you see, here you are again working for the Crisis Staff. Can you understand how people think that you are part of the Crisis Staff?" Your answer is: "Absolutely. I believe you can also get the impression that I cannot avoid doing certain things, because that way I would be arrested or I would be expelled or something would happen. But in doing all of these things that I was tasked with, to be humane and... That's why I'm convinced that you cannot bring a witness other than one that would come and lie." To which the lawyer says: "Well, it's one thing, Mr. Zaric, for you to say, `I did these things because I was ordered to do them, and if I didn't do them, I would be harmed or exchanged,' but you are telling us that you did not do these things at all." Now, your answer to all this, to put it in perspective is, you said: "If I was the assistant for civilian matters and for security and collected data and information of what was happening in the camps and what happened during the war, where do you see my responsibility? What's my problem? Where do you see my responsibility in that? Regardless of the fact that I was on orders from the Crisis Staff that sent me there."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no word "order" anywhere. That was simply added.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just read the statement in B/C/S to me, the last sentence from your question -- from your answer, sorry. Or better still, can you read the whole of your answer, which is the third paragraph on page 136. And just read it slowly so that it can be interpreted for us.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. Let me tell you. If I was an assistant for civilian affairs, for security, and collected information and intelligence about what had happened over there in the camps and what had gone there during the war, then what's my problem? Where do you find my responsibility there? Although or regardless of the fact that I had received it from the Crisis Staff and that it had sent me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say received it from the Crisis Staff, you mean the direction from the Crisis Staff to go there and collect information on what was happening in the camps and data, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said. And I had got it from the Crisis Staff. So where's my responsibility? If I did that part of my work honestly and correctly. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Maybe we could find out from Mr. Zaric if my learned friend be so kind, of which camps we are speaking. Where? Because simply just looking this part of statement, it's not so clear. Maybe it might be of assistance for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also one part of Mr. Zaric's statement was not correctly translated. He said: Even if I had got it from the Crisis Staff. These were his exact words, the way he just answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, maybe we could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say what was happening in the camps, what camps had the Crisis Staff sent you to gather information and collect data on, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not send me to any camps, but working in the territory of the Odzak municipality and while talking with people, with Serbs, those that I found there, I checked and collected information as to how they had fared in those camps whilst they were in Odzak, and there is a chapter in my book which contains the details about that investigation, and there is no need for me to go into that part of history before the Trial Chamber here. So it is about what the Serbs went through in the camps in the territory and municipality of Odzak at the time when the HVO forces had this part of the territory under their control. And this information was submitted to the international committee, and I'm sure that it can also be found in the office of the Tribunal, or rather, your Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You had responsibilities in the position, as you've described it there, as the assistant for civilian matters and for security to gather information on what was occurring in Odzak, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I did. And every information and every piece of intelligence I received, I transmitted to the chief of the military security administration body, Mr. Gojko Mackic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Crimes allegedly being committed by military personnel are security matters, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which army do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The one you happened to be working for in July, August, and September 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. I really don't understand what you are trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Crimes being -- crimes -- I withdraw that. Military personnel committing crimes is a disciplinary and morale and security issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes committed are crimes, are criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They are matters which affects discipline, morale, and security in a military brigade, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they're matters you would have been interested in, as the assistant commander for intelligence, reconnaissance, morale, and information; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. What period are we talking about? Because I haven't realised that we left the topic of Odzak. Are we talking about 2nd Posavina Brigade or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your position on the command staff, as the assistant commander for morale and information, crimes committed by military personnel were matters of concern to you within your duties, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could write such an information and then forward it. Of course it should -- such a problem should be in the information and then forwarded to the command and the commander should then forward it to security, so that everybody could do his part of the job. If the military did it. If you mean the period of time when I was with the 4th Detachment, I don't know which period of time you are now talking about. If you could be more precise. Because only then shall I be able to give a precise answer. You're asking me in general, I was deputy and assistant commander after the 1st of September and I really don't know what period of time you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were the deputy of the president -- to the president of the war council for security matters, as you've said in your statement P141 ter, page 91 --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Assistant or deputy. It doesn't matter that much. It's just a word. When you were in that position, in Odzak, crimes committed by -- allegedly committed by military personnel were matters within your domain, being in charge of security matters, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged in the collection of that information, and that was the only way for some people who have returned to the area from the camps to have interviews with them, and hear those distressing stories. Part of the Serbs who stayed after the HVO forces left, to talk with them and hear how they had fared in that area. And I wrote authentic and merely official notes and submitted them to my superior, and at the end of such note, I would always suggest that further information be gathered on the ground so that charges could be filed against the perpetrators of such severe crimes to relevant authorities, and that includes the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And you'd agree, of course, that crimes committed by military personnel against civilians fall within the categories you've just described, wouldn't you? But without a lengthy answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That would, of course, include the crime of rape, allegedly committed by military personnel against civilians in Odzak, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And I remember proceedings against them at the national court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You agree, of course, that rape committed by soldiers against civilians is a very serious crime, especially if committed by occupying soldiers, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it's a serious security and criminal issue which requires proper investigation and reporting; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if such information can be gathered. That is the worst part of the investigation. You know women who have some horrible experience are very seldom prepared to speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were working from the Hotel Odzak, there were complaints made to you that women had been -- Muslim women had been raped in Odzak, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one case, and I undertook measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was more than one case. You received complaints that a number of women were raped at the hotel at which you were working, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about several; I heard about the complaints of that one woman, one young woman who happens to be related to my wife, and she complained to me, and I told Mr. Mackic about that and he conducted an interview with them during the breakfast when you were there and he said: If such a similar incident happened anywhere, that is, that some of the soldiers forced them to go to bed with them or something, to let him know about it. And then he used his channels of command to inform the military administration. And as far as I know, after that intervention, I did not hear again about any other case of sexual assault. Of course, that does not mean that it didn't happen without me knowing about it, or perhaps that it was impossible to find out about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I take you to your statement to the Prosecutor on the 2nd of April, 1998. Can you please look at P141 ter at page 96, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Just look about two-thirds of the way down the page, where it says "Nancy," meaning Ms. Paterson, and she says: "We also heard that a number of women were raped at the hotel in Odzak, and they were taken there for forced labour. Do you know anything about those allegations?" Now, your response wasn't that there was only one person. You replied that earlier, just up the page, the previous answer. Your response to that, Mr. Zaric, was: "I also heard the same, but to be honest, I don't know. That kind of thing occurred also in my family, but persons who had gone through that do not want to talk about it, especially the women in a position where they were in a relationship or mothers that they wouldn't want their children to know. So it's very hard to assess to which extent it happened, because most women do not want to talk about it." What you said to the Prosecutor when she asked you was that you had heard that a number of women were raped at the hotel in Odzak. That's what you said there. What I want to ask you is: What did you do when these complaints were made to you that a number of women had been raped at the hotel where you were working from? What did you, Simo Zaric, in charge of security in Odzak, do about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this story, and when I told Mrs. Nancy, that is, I was being concrete. There have been rumours, but I'm talking about a specific case. When I interceded. I cannot act upon hearsay. When I receive the information, I reacted, and my reaction was of a productive nature, because Mr. Mackic immediately conducted interviews with those women and informed those in charge of such matters at the level of the military administration. And then I also explained how difficult it was to come by such information and explained what it is that had happened to Serb women from those fiery horses and all the rest of it that they had to go through and are reluctant to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you did nothing to investigate complaints of a number of women being raped in the hotel from which you were working in Odzak? Put it in the "too hard" basket, did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can ask me provocative things. I accept that.
