But what I wish to tell you is that I did not investigate that area, and when I learned something, my reaction was quick, was expedient, and submitted to the right place. During the month of my stay in the territory of Odzak, I visited, while not every village, I went to see what was the situation, I took stock of it, I took certain notes, I spoke with people in the -- on the ground, and so on and so forth, and I spent least of my time there in Odzak to consider that situation. And when I received that kind of information, that my reaction was expedient, correct, professional, and whatever you care to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you didn't send any reports on these rapes or your investigation of them to the Crisis Staff or to your military superiors, or Mr. Popovic, did you? It's a yes-or-no question, this one.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Mr. Mackic about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't send any to the Crisis Staff or Mr. Popovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. I was under no obligation to do that. My duty when I came there was to transmit all the intelligence information that I had to the office responsible for security in the military administration, and then he goes to the command, reports, and says what it is for that level. And at these administration meetings, you have Mr. Popovic present, not Mr. Simo Zaric. I was never at such meetings. I was the man who worked on the ground, who collected certain information as to what went on in that area and I took stock of the situation. I went to see my burnt-down village and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please. My question was: You didn't send it to Mr. Popovic. You're now going off somewhere else again. Now, move on from rapes. When you were in charge of security in Odzak, other serious crimes were committed, weren't they, namely, looting, forced labour, and forcing people, Muslims and Croats, to work in trench-digging on the front line. Those crimes were committed while you were in charge of security in Odzak, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever dug any trenches whilst I was in the territory of Odzak, nor was there any reason for it. That kind of -- that area was under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps, and no Muslim in the territory of Odzak went to dig trenches during that month that I was there, to my knowledge. Secondly, I was a man who collected intelligence. I made notes and submitted them to my superior. It was not my duty, nor did I have any authority to take some measures as Simo Zaric. But I had to, and that is what I did, write down what you've learned, turn it to a document, and submit it to your superior commander. I was not more than a month there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I asked you about trench-digging, forced labour, and looting. You've answered trench digging. Serious crimes of forced labour and looting occurred when you were in Odzak as the security chief, or in charge of security, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the chief. What sort of a chief was I? Don't attribute these posts to me which I never held.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I withdraw the word "chief." I'm sorry. This was a short way, because I'm getting a little bit frustrated by the length of your answers to very, very simple questions. I withdraw the word chief. Assistant commander for security. When you were there, serious crimes of looting and forced labour were committed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have expressed my opinion about looting, and I did not deny that there were people who failed to meet their work obligations. But what kind of responsibility are you attributing to me? I have nothing to do with this. Work obligation was under the direct authority of the Ministry of National Defence of the municipality of Samac. You had Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who was directly in charge of sending those people there. Whether that was illegal or not, let this Chamber decide, but I have nothing to do with it. I saw those people working in the streets, cleaning, washing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You too gave them assignments, didn't you, some of the people working -- who came to Odzak to do their what you call work obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, to one single person, did I give assignments. I will accept any responsibility -- I would accept responsibility had I ever sent someone to do work, but that is not true. All you have is lies told by certain witnesses. If that's what you mean, you can hold it against me, but they were lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your colleague and friend Vladimir Sarkanovic gave evidence about what was happening at the SUP. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, but would you please refresh my memory as to what parts you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we will have a problem with this. I mean, we already have a ruling by the Trial Chamber regarding the use of other witness's statement in potentially -- another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This is just absurd. I'm not -- it's absurd. I've only got half an hour left. You're standing up and making an objection about nothing. I'm not intending to impeach someone. Why do you object before you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I got wrong impression. Maybe I got wrong impression. But you have just -- starting quoting something that one witness said before this Tribunal to another witness. And it was not practiced, at least not in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And we already have this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A, I'm not attempting to impeach anyone; and B, it's between witnesses. Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You've said that you're not intending to use it for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, your friend and colleague Mr. Sarkanovic gave evidence, it's at page 16599, to the effect that -- this is the question. I asked him: "Everyone working in the police station was part of the terrible system, whether they wanted to be there or not, weren't they?" And he answered: "Yes, that's right." I then asked him: "It was obvious to you, as an educated man with a law degree and many years in the police an awareness of laws that there was a system of persecution being developed against the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac?" "Yes, you can say that." Now, your friend Mr. Sarkanovic has said in this court that there was a system of persecution being developed against the non-Serbs and that everyone working from the police station was aware of it. You too, Mr. Zaric, were working from the police station in terms of interrogating people in that period in May 1992, and you too were aware of the system of persecution, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not working for the police station, but I was aware of that fact. But I wasn't working for the police station. I was working as the assistant commander for security, connected to the 4th Detachment or the 5th Infantry Battalion, as it was after the transformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your position was, as both the chief of national security and the assistant commander for security connected to the 4th Detachment, was that you only interrogated the most important people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were the most senior person who was interrogating people from the police station, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about that. That's not true. This is an obstruction of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that, but it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The interrogations you conducted were -- I withdraw that. Interrogations conducted in the SUP in May -- April and May 1992 were conducted by both military and civilian interrogators, weren't they, that is you, the military, Mr. Sarkanovic and Cancarevic from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic and Mr. Savic were there from the civilian authorities. I don't know about Cancarevic. He may have been there too. You are mentioning this name for the first time as an investigator. In Bosanski Samac I only had an interview with Mr. Tihic and in Brcko I had three interviews with Mr. Nalic and the two Bicic brothers. All my official interviews boiled down to those four names. The official notes and the statements I took have been shown here, and I'm glad that some of the witnesses were here and they said how I behaved during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As an experienced former chief of public security station, you knew, as of April and May 1992, that the prisoners in the SUP and the TO were in no fit physical or psychological condition to be interrogated, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all. I can say that they were in a difficult situation, but I told you of an authentic case when Mr. Tihic was beaten up. When I interviewed him and came back, I said Mr. Tihic, I suggest that we not talk, because I saw that the man was beating, that he had been beaten up, and he begged me to stay and complete the interview, because he said: I'll be back and they will beat me again. And that was the only reason I stayed there with him. It never occurred to me to make use of their unequal position to extort some sort of evidence and to fit into some sort of scenario of something you call planned and so on. This cannot be attributed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You only interrogated non-Serbs, didn't you, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you submitted reports on your interrogations to your military superiors, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I sent all my reports to my superior, Captain Makso Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At that stage, when you were sending the reports, the military, that is, the JNA, and the paramilitaries and the Crisis Staff were in control of Bosanski Samac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are making a connection I will never agree with, nor can agree with, of course. You want to put the JNA on the same level as the volunteers who committed crimes or the Crisis Staff, which imposed a certain policy we did not agree with. These three things cannot go together, Mr. Prosecutor, at least as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who are you suggesting controlled Bosanski Samac at the time you submitted your reports to your military superiors, given that the JNA was controlling the banks of the town, had tanks there, soldiers on the streets, the Crisis Staff had proclaimed a state of emergency and seized control of all the civilian administration, soldiers were guarding the vital facilities. Who do you say was in control of Bosanski Samac at that time if it wasn't the JNA, Crisis Staff, and paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I refer to the fact that there was war, I know for certain that members of the 4th Detachment, as part of the JNA, had the task to be on the front defence lines, so that the enemies from Croatia and the HVO from the surrounding area would be prevented from entering into town. The civilian authorities in the town were the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board, and as for control of the town in the sense of law and order, that was done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, paramilitary forces -- Serbian paramilitary forces took control of Bosanski Samac's vital facilities in the middle of the night, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And these were the same Serbian paramilitary forces of the types that you were aware had taken control of Zvornik, Bijeljina, and Vlasenica, in the preceding weeks in Bosanski Brod, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no Serb forces in Bosanski Brod. They were the forces of the regular army of Croatia. I don't know whether the people who came to Samac had been in Bijeljina and Zvornik before that. I really don't know that. I can't say that. But I do know that they came from training in the area of Ilok, which belonged, as far as territory goes, to the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the takeover there had been a democratically elected government, hadn't there, of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Serb paramilitary forces, Serbian paramilitary forces, could be seen as infantry shock troops, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 30 of them? Well, if they can be called that, I don't mind. They were always on the move, so they can be seen as a sort of infantry component. During the war, I never saw them using artillery weapons or something of that sort, so one might say that they had an infantry component.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Shock troops are those that go forward and seize something ahead of the larger force, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military strategist, to be quite honest. I know that if we exclude the act of the takeover of Samac, and I have been very clear about my opinion of that, later on, the police and the special units they set up went to all the places where the HVO was trying to pierce the front line to break through, and I know that six of them were killed and were sent off in coffins to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A mere few hours after the Serbian paramilitary forces took control and seized the vital facilities in Bosanski Samac, the JNA -- sorry, and started collecting weapons from the citizens, the JNA completed the task, didn't they, of collecting weapons from the citizens?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "a mere few hours." Yes, I agree with that. The 4th Detachment had part of that task, and we did that in the fourth quarter of the town of Samac, in that local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff proclaimed a state of emergency and took control of the administration imposing Serb-only rule, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And this Serb-only government took persecutory measures, as you've outlined in the 13 signatories, P127, against the non-Serbs, starting from day one, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part of the non-Serb population only in relation to them can we speak of the extreme measure you call persecution. I'm referring to those who, in my view, were taken prisoner, who were put into an unequal position, and so on. All the others who left through the Red Cross, and in other ways, I do understand that it was not purely due to their own wish, but we couldn't call that persecution. Because as far as I know, at the very beginning of the war, over 30.000 Croats were not in the part that was held by the JNA [as interpreted]. This was all outside Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the number that we have here in the transcript is not the one that Mr. Zaric mentioned. On page --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you say, Mr. Zaric. I'll clear it up. What did you say, Mr. Zaric, if not 30.000?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that over 10.000 Croats in the first days --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said 10, not 30. That's all I want to know. We move along from there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've established that. I'm moving on. Now, Mr. Zaric, Mr. Pantelic, a few days ago, last week, talked about a military coup or a putsch. That was in effect what had happened in Bosanski Samac, non-elected military armed forces had seized control of the town and municipality from the democratically elected government. It was nothing more than a military coup, was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you can compare that. You're comparing a military putsch in relation to the information of the 13? Are you putting that on the same level?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. The takeover of the town, the vital facilities, by armed forces seizing power and putting in place a new Serb-only government. That was a military coup, or a putsch, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I wouldn't call it a military coup. It was simply a takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: By military means, by arms, wasn't it, against a democratically elected government?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what name will be given to it here, but what I knew of the takeover of the town of Samac, well, I've said that and I abide by what I said. If you feel that this is a military coup, you can defend your opinion, but that's not what I saw. That's not how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Forcible takeover? You'd agree with that? I think you already have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. This is what I was about to say, that we've been through this with Mr. Simo Zaric before. I'm wondering about going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm trying to finish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't have to repeat what you've gone over with Mr. Zaric before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the JNA's -- sorry. What the JNA did in collecting weapons and doing nothing to seize control from the paramilitaries or prevent them consolidating power allowed the Crisis Staff to take control, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a conclusion can be drawn if one does not accept the fact as to what the task of the 4th Detachment was and how we carried it out. When I say that, it means that on the 17th, acting on orders from our commander, we went to the peripheral parts of town and took those areas where we had reason to expect the enemy to come and take over Samac, the municipality of Samac was the only one not under HVO control in the area. But I would not be sitting here had they taken control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Knowing of the takeover, the discriminatory takeover on ethnic grounds, you participated in supervising the collection of weapons the following day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out the task assigned to me. I did not think about the thesis you are trying to advocate here. I thought it was logical that someone should not be shooting at us from behind our backs while we were on the combat lines, and we were watching out for the enemy, for an enemy attack from the direction we were expecting an attack from. That is how I acted on the front line. And wherever the 4th Detachment took part in the collection of weapons, we did this in a very proper manner, a very correct manner, without any incidents and without irritating the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Knowing that Serbian paramilitary forces had taken over the town and were installing a Serb-only government, knowing that, you participated by -- sorry, you, the following day, participated by supervising the collection of weapons throughout the town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct, for that reason. Across the Bosna, from the village of Prud, was a paramilitary formation from Croatia which had arrived with Mr. Cavka, and we thought he might enter the town from that direction. The weapons we collected on the outskirts was that reason, because there were a lot of people in the town with various standpoints who are members of different military and paramilitary structures. And it was very dangerous not to take some security measures and protect our soldiers on the defence line. In my view, this act of protection of the soldiers on the line was legitimate and any army in any country of the world would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The JNA acted in coordination with the paramilitaries after the morning of the 17th of April, 1992, in consolidating power in Bosanski Samac, by stationing tanks, putting soldiers on the streets, and guarding the facilities that the paramilitaries had taken over and installed the Crisis Staff in, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct, sir, because a real war broke out on the following day. Samac was a real hell. We were shelled from every direction. Shells fell relentlessly on our town every day. We had to fight. We had an open enemy who did not conceal his intentions. It never occurred to me to sit and wait to see what destiny had in store for me. But I did not do anything bad against the other people who stayed with us, be assured of that. But Samac was shelled every day. We were attacked from every direction. 138 people were killed in the town. These were civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The thousands of heavily armed members of the 17th Tactical Group, or 17th Corps, with their heavy weapons and artillery, did nothing to assist the democratically elected government restore itself to power, did they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This democratic government you are talking about set up their own municipalities. They went to their own areas and they were no longer a part of our area, except for one part, which refers to people from the SDA who were detained. Because right away the Croatian municipality of Domaljevac, as part of Samac, was set up, and all the Croatian villages joined it, and Prud fell under Odzak, which was held by the HVO forces. So the presidents of the former municipalities and the Executive Board and the legitimate government, that was their democratic option, and they did something similar. Bosnia was a great evil, and responsibility cannot be attributed to only one nation. But we Serbs do bear part of the responsibility, and this is not contentious. Let those who are responsible answer for it, but you cannot say that the entire Serbian people are to blame for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think I actually did, but are you saying -- do we take it from your last answer that the things you've referred to justify military takeover on ethnic grounds, ethnic cleansing and persecution?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot attribute that to me. You can only say that. But this cannot be part of my being.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because knowing, as you have told us, of the system which had been put in place after the 17th of April, 1992, that's the discriminatory system, you, Mr. Zaric, participated in it by interrogating prisoners in the SUP and at Brcko, prisoners of the Serb discriminatory authorities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I interrogated people. I learned from those interviews how they were -- how they had been getting ready as our enemies. I undertook no repressive measures against them. I conducted correct interviews and I learned how the paramilitary HDZ and SDA formations had been getting ready to take over their part of authority in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina who seemed to me too little for everybody at the time, and until that time I thought it was just the right size and the dearest place of all, of course, with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This persecutory system in which you participated required people to interrogate the prisoners, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody can tell me, ever, that I did something as extremist as persecution. Mr. Re, please. My daughter and my grandchildren live in Croatia to this day, so I should be like a criminal, like a grandfather and a father to persecute those Croats that my daughter married or -- and so on and so forth, so I should be -- I'd be a monster, not a man. Secondly, my political views and my options are so clear in that regard that I -- that from the very first day I've been fighting against that injustice. I had strength enough in 1992 to write the information when I wasn't aware that a conflict would break out [as interpreted]. That was a courage tantamount to death but I wasn't afraid of it. And I said it served you as a foundation so you could conduct a case against the Samac group and now you're trying to impute to me that I engaged in some kind of persecutions. So that means that there can be no Serb who is honest and who took an honest and correct position towards the war. I think I belonged into the -- into -- amongst those people who had a very correct attitude towards it all in those distressing times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have something here in the transcript which is not what Mr. Zaric said, on page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said: I had strength enough in 1992 to write the information. When I wasn't aware, here it says that the conflict would break out. He said when I wasn't aware that this Tribunal would be established. This is what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Zaric has heard that. Do you agree that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. Yes, precisely, Madam President. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, different people in this persecutory system had different roles to perform, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I take it that's a yes. The Crisis Staff had its role to perform in issuing edicts, persecutory edicts, and in working with Mr. Todorovic and the paramilitaries to have hundreds of Muslims and Croats arrested; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, I don't know if it's up to me to pass judgements after so many statements by witnesses on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, actually, Mr. Re. I was about to say that you are simply going through what we've been through. This witness -- the accused has also been through these, and I'm wondering why --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get to a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, then get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the point I'm making here, so that there's no confusion, is everybody in that system had a different role to play, and once people were arrested on discriminatory grounds and detained, the system of persecution required trained interrogators to interview detainees. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you. They were interrogated when [indiscernible] wanted to and they also beat them. And when I interrogated them, I treated them correctly and professionally, and there is a big difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is that by interrogating these people who had been arrested on discriminatory grounds and detained based upon their ethnicity, you, Mr. Zaric, were participating in the system and contributing to it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never in that context. No. I carried out an order and I did a part of the job, and the information I came by indicates a very high degree of responsibility of those that I interrogated, both politically and in any other sense. But it wasn't my task further on. My task was to conduct the interview, and what I did, I did correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And further, by accepting the position as chief of national security for the Crisis Staff and interrogating people in that capacity, and by travelling to Belgrade with the Crisis Staff in that capacity, you were contributing to the system of persecution and participating in it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only you can invent a thing like that and say, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And similarly, by accepting the position, your appointment by the same persecutory Crisis Staff, to the deputy to the war council or assistant to the war council in Odzak and continuing the work of the Crisis Staff, that persecutory body, you too were participating in and contributing to the persecution against the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot but admire your obstructions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Tadic judgement, paragraph 110, says: "The JNA, and in particular, its air force, actively cooperated with and assisted the paramilitary units in 1991 and 1992 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and liberally supplied them with arms and equipment." That's what a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal has found. That's what happened in Bosanski Samac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It happened in Prijedor, as far as I know, Tadic comes from Prijedor. If that's the gentleman that you mean when you say "Tadic," because I'm aware of this Tadic who is with me, but he has not been sentenced yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's a different Tadic, and it refers to a general statement of the whole situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992. Does that assist? It's not talking specifically about Prijedor. It's the general, saying this is what the JNA air force did. It armed the paramilitaries and actively cooperated with them and liberally supplied them with arms and equipment. And that's exactly what happened in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened elsewhere, but what happened in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality, or, more correctly, in the town of Samac, such an association of the Yugoslav People's Army with paramilitary formations has absolutely no common connotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the Trial Chamber is of the view that you have nothing new to work on or to ask Mr. Simo Zaric. You have covered everything, that's why you are now going through what you have been through before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just check with my colleagues to make sure that they feel that I haven't left any stone unturned at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I hope they won't support repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sure they won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours and my colleagues are ad idem on this issue. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I have a minute to consult my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave. Thank you. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, may I have the same opportunity, in order to save the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, officially now, Your Honours. I have only one question for Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zaric, this morning, whilst you were answering questions of the Prosecution - I don't have the transcript in front of me, but I noted down - the Prosecutor was showing you a part of book referring to Mr. Blagoje Simic, saying that you had mentioned him, and your answer to the Prosecutor was that Blagoje Simic was surrounded by well-known players who already have become well known nationalists, and you mentioned Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Simeun Simic, Bozo Ninkovic. You even said that these are individuals who had already had national and even -- who had embraced national or nationalistic policy. That was roughly your answer to the Prosecutor. And with regard to my client, because we know he was a member of the Crisis Staff for a while. And you spoke about the Crisis Staff. Would you say that Miroslav Tadic was one of those men who were Serb nationalists and who had been described as such and who also were in the company of Mr. Blagoje Simic in that context?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tadic could not be called a part of that circle. That's for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To sum Prosecution's questions related to the arrest of Sulejman Tihic and other front men of the SDA in Samac, you said that the grounds for their arrest was the fact that they were Muslims and also their political affiliation. Do you remember that, when the Prosecutor asked you about that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something to that effect. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in any event, you were also talking about some other documents that had been found in the police station, and I'm referring to the military organisation of the SDA, their staff, and so on and so forth. Now, it does not seem quite logical to me now, regardless of what Todorovic and his men did. My question is as follows: It does not seem quite logical to me, if we know that there was this document, this plan, and you personally were aware of some wrongful activities even before mid-April 1992. What is the reason, then? What is the ground for their arrest? Since you gave two answers which are contradictory, will you please opt for a more specific one, and more objective, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I know that in the police station, especially Mr. Todorovic, and I could even say in part some inspectors, when it came to this subject, their starting point was the fact that the war plan prepared by the SDA served as a ground to take people in. And in the beginning I didn't know it, I found it out later, I must say that I wasn't even aware that Mr. Tihic owned illegal weapons, but later on it was unmasked. And they always claimed that that was the chief reason why he had been brought in. But in this other context, when I spoke, I meant goodwill which was shown. I remember this interview as if it happened yesterday. But Mr. Blagoje Simic was quite ready for Mr. Tihic and me and Mr. Todorovic to get together and to discuss Mr. Tihic's release. Because until the day before, Mr. Tihic was Mr. Simic's first political partner, because they shared the government. They were in coalition with the SDA. And now I tried to bring in some democratic trends to my assistants and I thought that his position as a politician played a decisive role that that was why he was there and I thought that Mr. Simic's prestige should perhaps prevail and that Mr. Tihic and others holding those political views could be released from the prison. It is along those lines that I was thinking at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, Mr. Zaric, they were at the garrison in Brcko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after that, they went to the military airfield in Batajnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, they went to Bijeljina, and it was after that that I -- that information reached me that they had gone to Batajnica, and you're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that it was some high-ranking security structures who did that, because they must have had some reason to conduct further interviews with them in Batajnica. Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't go into that, but I have to remind you of that major, Major Nikola, who used to come with Mr. Stevan. He came from the security bodies of the AFAAD [phoen]. Whether he was trying to manipulate something or was trying truly to get some statements from this or some others who were taken by helicopter through the territory of Serbia. Whether they deserved such treatment, whether they had to go, I'd rather not go into that. But it is a fact that the high-ranking instances of the military security from that wing of the Yugoslav People's Army which I called the air force and the anti-aircraft defence had a hand in the transfer of those people from the territory of Samac or more correctly from the territory of Republika Srpska at the time to the territory of Yugoslavia or Batajnica, as you have concretely mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please slow down, because there is interpretation going on.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So let us conclude. You mentioned a certain Major Nikola, and he came from the security service of the air force, who was in Stevan Todorovic's office in April 1992, who followed what was going on there and then did something. Is that correct what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And he was pulling some strings there, and that is why I'm drawing my conclusions, but I think they are quite grounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that in those -- in this communication with the security service of the AFAAD, with this Major Nikola that Dr. Simic was playing any role in all that? Because I think that you are quite well informed.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really didn't hear about any link between them. I never had an opportunity there. I never sat with them together, nor did I overhear what they talked about. That Nikola never left the station and he was always in the company with Mr. Todorovic, with Mr. Crni, and Mr. Srecko Radovanovic. That was that team which, conditionally speaking, was solving the fate that you asked me about, I mean of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Today there was also talk about a programme, or rather, an interview for the TV television.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you remember, Colonel Nikolic, in his testimony here, explained how they had first come to see him and that he had then sent them on to you to make that programme, that is, that was his -- in this way he ordered you to take part in this programme. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had already had a talk with them and that I should get ready. I didn't have much time, but in that little time that I had, I got ready and gave my part of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not to listen to this tape again, will you please try to clarify something. When you participated in that programme, did you and other participants have a script, have something from which you would be reading questions and answers? Did any of the participants, and I mean you, Mr. Tihic, Mr. Coner, I believe, Nalic, and all the others, did any one of you have a script prepared in advance? I'm talking physically. Did you have any notes as to what they should be answering?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to tell that to the Prosecutor. There were no notes whatsoever. The journalist called Minja, I don't know his last name, was asking questions directly to each one of the participants in that interview. There was nothing predirected. I didn't see any questions which had been preset. And when I participated -- when I participated in the interview, then I merely used documentation from the war plan of the SDA in order to show that there was a prepared war option, and so on and so forth. So there was no script. There was no scenario. This journalist didn't have it and he did it just professionally, like any other journalist who is interviewing somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And my next question in this relation: Did Blagoje Simic personally, and do you have any knowledge about that, did he participate in the organisation of that programme, its preparation, or in any other concrete way? I'm talking about him personally, not about others.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that. I know that on the eve of that they were together with Mr. Todorovic and walked around the town, but I have absolutely no information that they had been to the Crisis Staff or had any conversations with Mr. Blagoje Simic. I really do not have such information in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "they," you mean journalists of the TV television?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely whom I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you about another thing. Now we are talking about the [indiscernible], about the chain of command in the police of Republika Srpska. You already told us and that is not in dispute that there was a regional centre in Doboj was Superior [indiscernible] before the corridor was set up because Samac was rounded then but it was the regional centre in Bijeljina was in charge of them. I'm talking about the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. I was just waiting for the transcript. Now, Mr. Zaric, in view of the well-known details concerning the wrongful conduct of Stevan Todorovic and his policemen, those volunteers and so on, at that time, did you - and when I say you, I don't mean you personally, I mean your colleagues from the 17th Tactical Group, that is Simeunovic and others, those who were above you, did they report about Todorovic's omissions and crimes? Did you report about them to the relevant bodies in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska? Because I'm sure you will agree with me that the security bodies and the civilians do cooperate up to a certain degree. Now, do you have any knowledge that the Superior Command drew the attention to the omissions in the police work of Stevan Todorovic and his policemen? If you know that, will you please tell us. Were there any interventions? Was there anything said?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that should be the route to take. They should be -- done. But I do not know in what direction this information was sent later on. But to me it sounds quite logical for the Superior Command, that is, the first command superior to me, that is the 17th Tactical Group, it was to inform the 17th Corps or the BK [phoen] Corps in Bijeljina, and quite sure that if we are to prevent crimes then the civilian and the military security need to cooperate and since they were talking and I'm referring to my structure, since they had detailed information because I really wrote very detailed reports as to what was going on in Samac, so therefore they could take their chains of command to report to relevant authorities in the ministry and then to my mouth. It would be logical for them to take certain steps, of course unless there were people in the ministry, such as Ostoja Minic, who was in the meeting, but you can't expect such people to do anything, because he was the same as Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But it seems to me, even though it goes beyond the indictment, but because of some perhaps -- it might be perhaps of some indirect relevance. Do you know if minister Tomo Kovac, at some point, perhaps in 1994, 1995, perhaps did something in this regard and dismissed Stevan Todorovic? Do you remember any such activities of the Ministry of the Interior? Of course, if you know anything about it, if not, you don't.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I know that he was dismissed and we all breathed with relief then and we all asked ourselves question: Well, did it have to take so long for somebody to see what was happening and do something about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, time for our adjournment or break today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. This is the end of the session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is the end of the session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of May 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.45 p.m.,
